ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Simplified overview of the overall analysis pipeline employed in our study (acceptance-and avoidance-related) psychedelic experiences. Wolff et al. (2022) collected data from 2,078 participants; after applying the exclusion criteria of the original study, data from 1,829 participants remain (997 English-and 832 German-speaking), who each reported on one psychedelic experience (clearly discernible psychoactive effects) following the use of different substances (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, or ayahuasca).
table.formatted: Simplified overview of the overall analysis pipeline employed in our study (acceptance-and avoidance-related) psychedelic experiences. <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Wolff et al. (2022)</ref> collected data from 2,078 participants; after applying the exclusion criteria of the original study, data from 1,829 participants remain (997 English-and 832 German-speaking), who each reported on one psychedelic experience (clearly discernible psychoactive effects) following the use of different substances (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, or ayahuasca).

table.text: Participants were instructed that both positive and negative experiences could be reported on.
After questions on demographic data and mental health issues/diagnoses, participants were asked to describe the psychedelic experience in a free-text format, either in English or German.
A total of 1,195 volunteers began the survey and 512 provided informed consent to participate.

Of these, 269 participants were excluded for the following reasons: not meeting inclusion criteria (n = 90), discontinuation of the survey before completing the PCL-5 items (n = 176), free-text responses indicating a lack of genuine participation (e.g., "just reading"; n = 2), or exceeding the recommended relative speed index cut-off (> 2) without any indication of engagement in free-text comments (n = 1).
table.formatted: Of these, 269 participants were excluded for the following reasons: not meeting inclusion criteria (n = 90), discontinuation of the survey before completing the PCL-5 items (n = 176), free-text responses indicating a lack of genuine participation (e.g., "just reading"; n = 2), or exceeding the recommended relative speed index cut-off (> 2) without any indication of engagement in free-text comments (n = 1).

table.text: Participants were asked to report on this "particularly challenging or traumatic psychedelic experience", and additionally provided responses on a series of questions and questionnaires.

In a modification of the original instructions, participants were asked to rate their symptoms not over the past month, but specifically with reference to the month they found most challenging following their psychedelic experience.
Participants were asked three questions to which they were instructed to provide free-text responses: 1) Acute Symptoms.

Open-ended free-text responses function fundamentally different as they are inherently personalized: Depending on how open the questions are worded, participants are completely free to produce whatever they themselves deem relevant or informative.

ethics_check.report:

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. table.text: For the change in psychological flexibility (AAQ-II), we obtain a cross-validated R² = .379 for the baseline model (median α = 0.0, λ = 3.94), a cross-validated R² = .410 for the extended-by-text model (median α = 0.0, λ = 6.28), and consequently a ∆R² = .030 (95% CI [.011, .050], t(99) = 3.09, p = .003; an increase of 3.0% in absolute terms and of 8.0% in relative terms).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: Thus, in the pre-specified test of the extended-by-text model containing both responses, we find a ∆R² = .006 (95% CI [-.011, .022], t(99) = 0.70, p = .486), which is not reliably different from zero.

table.sample_values: | Ich habe danach viel über meine Rolle als Mutter nachgedacht und darüber, was ich meinen Kindern vorlebe. Ich bin kritischer mit mir selbst geworden. | It gave me a sense that life is precious and worth living. I had been very low for a long time and this was like the sun coming out. |   |

I went to a licensed psilocybin service center, which I chose specifically because I wanted it to be safe and legal. I had a preparation session with a facilitator, a calm older woman, and she was great. I wanted to work on a general sense of anxiety that I've had my whole life. I took a high dose, 35mg of psilocybin, in a comfortable room with music.

The first hour was wonderful. Colours, music that felt like it was inside me, a deep sense of relaxation. I remember thinking 'this is going to be easy'.

Then, without any warning, I couldn't breathe. It felt like there was water in my lungs. I sat up and gasped and the facilitator came over. I tried to tell her I was drowning and I couldn't get the words out. And then I was underwater. Not imagining it, being there. I was a small child, maybe three or four, and I was at the bottom of a pool looking up at the light and the shadows of people on the surface. I was kicking and nobody came. I swallowed water. My chest was burning. I knew I was going to die.

I've since learned from my mother that I nearly drowned in a hotel pool when I was three and that my uncle pulled me out. I had no conscious memory of this at all. Nobody in my family had ever mentioned it.

In the session room I apparently was gasping and clawing at my throat. The facilitator stayed calm and kept talking to me, but at some point she was worried enough about my breathing that she called the on-site supervisor, who checked my oxygen with a finger monitor. It was normal, 98 percent. They told me that. It didn't matter. In my body I was drowning and it went on and on.

Then the drowning turned into something else. I was no longer a child, I was no longer anyone. The water became a huge dark space and I was dissolving into it. It felt like the end of me, and I fought it with everything I had. The more I fought, the worse it got. The facilitator kept saying 'let it move through you', and eventually, because I had no strength left, I stopped fighting. And for a moment there was a strange quiet, like floating. That moment was peaceful. But then the panic came back in waves for the rest of the session, maybe another two hours. Each wave I was underwater again.

By the end I was lying on the floor wrapped in a blanket, completely exhausted, my throat raw from gasping. The facilitator sat with me until I could walk. My partner picked me up. I didn't speak in the car. At home I took a shower and had a panic attack when the water hit my face.

I want to say that the facilitators did everything right. This wasn't their fault. But it was the most frightening thing I've ever been through. | Mushrooms, about 3g, at home with my roommate. I got stuck in a loop where I kept 'waking up' from the trip, thinking it was over, and then realising I was still in it. Each time I woke up, things were slightly different, the furniture moved, my roommate's clothes changed colour. I counted maybe 40 loops. I became convinced I'd never wake up for real, that I'd be stuck in a nested dream forever. My roommate kept telling me where I was, but each time I thought he was part of the dream. | I want to start by saying that I was experienced with psychedelics, I'd done mushrooms maybe 15 times, and I thought I knew what I was doing. That arrogance is part of the story.

It was October and I decided to go on a solo hike in a national park and take a large dose of mushrooms, around 5 grams, at a spot I'd been to before, a viewpoint about two hours' walk from the car park. My plan was to sit there for the peak and walk back in the afternoon. I told nobody where I was going. My father had died that summer and I wanted to 'connect' with him and with nature.

I took the mushrooms around 11am. The come-up was very fast and strong. Within 40 minutes I couldn't stand properly. The landscape started to breathe and pulse, and the trees looked like they were made of light. For a while it was overwhelming but beautiful. Then I saw my father. Not like a hallucination exactly, but I knew he was there, sitting on a rock nearby. He looked sick, the way he looked in the hospital at the end. He didn't say anything. He just looked at me with this terrible sadness. I started to cry and I tried to go to him and I fell down a small slope and hurt my ankle.

After that, everything turned. The light was going (I didn't realise how late it was, I'd lost all sense of time), and the trees around me became threatening. I heard voices in the wind, and I felt that the forest was angry that I was there. I started to believe I was going to die there, that my father had come to take me with him. Then I lost the sense of being a person at all. I was just fear, spread across the whole forest. I don't know how long this lasted.

When I became somewhat aware again it was dark. I was cold, my ankle was swollen and I was still tripping. My phone had almost no battery and no signal. I tried to walk back but I couldn't find the trail. I kept hearing things moving in the bushes, and every shadow looked like a figure. I sat down under a tree and wrapped myself in my rain jacket and shook all night. I was convinced I would freeze to death, and part of me thought I deserved it for not being there more for my dad.

At first light I started walking and eventually found a forest road. A ranger in a truck picked me up around 9am. I was hypothermic and had a sprained ankle, and I spent a night in a small hospital. The doctors were kind, but I was too ashamed to tell them about the mushrooms at first. When I finally told my sister what had happened, she cried and said she could have lost two family members in one year. | High dose of LSD alone. I became convinced I was in hell and that I'd been there forever. My life before was a memory implanted to make the torment worse. I lay on my floor for 8 hours seeing flames. | Ich habe auf einer Silvesterparty LSD genommen. Um Mitternacht ging das Feuerwerk los, und es war fuer mich wie ein Bombenangriff. Ich habe mich auf den Boden geworfen und die Haende ueber den Kopf gelegt. Jeder Knall war eine Explosion, jedes Licht ein Einschlag. Meine Freunde haben gelacht, weil sie dachten, ich mache Spass, bis sie gesehen haben, dass ich weine. Ich habe mich in der Wohnung im Bad eingeschlossen und bin bis zum Morgen nicht herausgekommen.

In the months after, I had panic attacks that always involved breathing. I'd suddenly feel like I couldn't get air and I'd gasp. It would happen in the shower, when I put my face in water, when I had a cold and my nose was blocked, and sometimes for no reason at all, lying in bed. I avoided swimming completely, which I used to love. I had nightmares about water. I also had some days of feeling very far away from myself.

Grounding techniques help in the moment: cold water on my face, strong mints, naming objects. Running helps. Playing music helped once I got back to it, though the first months back in the band were hard.

T, my old housemate, has stayed a close friend. Talking to him about that night, and about ordinary things, still helps.

What didn't help: R's insistence that I'd had a spiritual awakening, and forums where people describe DP as permanent.

I'm functional and mostly okay, but it's still there. | Breathing exercises and slowly going to parties again with a friend who knew. It worked, mostly. | Ich habe mir selbst Unterstützung gesucht, bei einer Beratungsstelle für Angehörige von Menschen in psychischen Krisen. Das hat mir geholfen, meine eigene Angst ernst zu nehmen und nicht nur auf ihn zu schauen. Er hat eine Therapie angefangen, und wir haben ein paar Paargespräche gemacht. Heute geht es uns beiden besser.

I talked to a friend who is an art historian, who explained the paintings to me, their history and what they meant to people at the time. That helped make them less scary. Later I went back to the museum with her, sober, in the morning when it was quiet. I also did some CBT exercises from a self-help book for the general anxiety. It's mostly fine now. | Ich habe mit einer Psychologin über meine Gesundheitsangst gesprochen und eine kurze Verhaltenstherapie gemacht. Dabei habe ich gelernt, mein Herzklopfen nicht mehr ständig zu überprüfen. Der Kardiologe hat mir außerdem ein Langzeit-EKG gemacht, was mich beruhigt hat. Langsam wieder mit Sport anzufangen, erst Spazierengehen, dann leichtes Joggen, war am wichtigsten. | The hospital treated my frostbite, and I saw a physiotherapist for months to learn to walk properly again. Psychologically, I was resistant to getting help because I felt I'd brought it on myself. My partner eventually insisted. I found a psychologist who works with people after accidents and medical trauma. We focused on the episodes of the white field, using grounding and gradual exposure to bright light and white rooms. I also took an SSRI for about a year for the depression.

I've stopped taking psychedelics entirely, which was a big decision because they had been part of my identity for ten years. Letting go of that identity has been part of the healing.

My friend and I eventually talked it all through. He said he'd been terrified of finding me dead. That conversation was hard but important.

I still struggle in winter. | Ich habe eine Trauerbegleiterin aufgesucht, mit der ich über meine Großeltern gesprochen habe. Das hat mir geholfen, die Schuldgefühle zu verarbeiten und mich an die schönen Zeiten mit ihnen zu erinnern. Irgendwann konnte ich ihr Grab wieder besuchen. Ich habe dort einen Brief vorgelesen, den ich ihnen geschrieben hatte. Das war sehr befreiend. | I journaled about it for a few weeks and then talked to my mum about my first year. She told me I'd had colic and that she'd been at the end of her rope, and sometimes had to put me down and leave the room to calm herself. It made sense and was oddly comforting to hear.

After the hospital I was referred to a community mental health team. I had a care coordinator who visited every two weeks, and a psychiatrist who prescribed an antidepressant and, for the first two months, a low-dose antipsychotic, which I think helped with the presence. After that I had a course of CBT with a psychologist. She was very good. She helped me understand that the presence was a kind of threat-detection gone into overdrive, and we did exercises like sitting with my back to the door on purpose.

Living with my parents was hard but also stabilising. My mum and I eventually talked properly, and she told me how scared she'd been. That helped us both.

I started volunteering at an animal shelter, which got me out of the house and gave me structure. Eventually I got a new job.

Unhelpful: reading forums where people described never recovering from bad trips. Also, a friend who suggested a 'healing' mushroom trip to undo the bad one.

I'm a lot better now, two years later. I still don't like mirrors in the evening. | Ich habe eine Therapie begonnen, auch um zu lernen, wie ich meine Schwester unterstützen kann, ohne mich selbst zu überfordern. Sie macht selbst eine Traumatherapie. Wir reden viel miteinander. Mit unseren Eltern haben wir inzwischen auch gesprochen. Den Onkel sehen wir nicht mehr. | | Keine Horrorfilme mehr, das war die ganze Behandlung. | We talked a lot about it on the rest of the trip and after. White noise machine at night helped. It faded.

I saw a therapist after the breakup, partly for the depression and partly to understand what had happened that night. She helped me see that the mushrooms had amplified real issues but also distorted them. I've started dating again, carefully. My ex and I had one conversation a year later, which was sad but healing. | Ich habe eine Verhaltenstherapie gemacht, die mir bei der Angst in Menschenmengen etwas geholfen hat. Ich übe noch, z.B. mit vollen Bahnen. Festivals sind für mich vorbei. | I went back into an eating disorder day programme for three months. My treatment team was supportive and didn't judge me for the mushrooms, which I was afraid of. I'm in outpatient therapy now and have been stable for a year. I've told everyone in my recovery group about this, so that nobody else gets the same idea from a friend. | Wir haben beide viel darüber geredet, auch mit seiner Familie. Ein paar Gespräche bei einer Trauerberatung haben mir geholfen, das Erlebte einzuordnen. | Reading Buddhist texts on suffering, meditation, and volunteering at the hospice. Talking to the hospice chaplain. These help, but the dread hasn't fully gone.

Once I'd told my husband, things started to move. My GP referred me to a psychologist, who recognised quickly that I was having intrusive thoughts and that they are very common and don't mean anything about who I am. That was a huge relief. We did CBT for the intrusive thoughts, with exposure, which was terrifying at first, for example spending time in the classroom and allowing the thoughts to come without leaving. Over months it became easier.

My husband and I did couples therapy, which helped us reconnect and talk about the infertility honestly. I also started an antidepressant, after discussing it with the fertility clinic.

I wrote to the retreat about what happened. They were kind and apologetic, which I didn't expect, and offered a free integration session, which I declined.

I went back to teaching after five months. I'm doing much better. We're still trying for a baby, and I still have hard days, but I no longer believe what the trip told me. | Ich habe ein paar Stunden Therapie gemacht, das hat bei der Schreckhaftigkeit etwas geholfen. Silvester meide ich weiterhin. | | Nothing was necessary, honestly. | Once my friend named it as trauma, I found a therapist who knew about psychedelic harms. We worked with somatic approaches, to help me feel at home in my body again, and later with EMDR on the images of being torn apart. I also did gradual exposure to dogs, with a friend's very calm old labrador. I distanced myself from the retreat and the community around it, which was hard because many of my friends were part of it. I'm much better now, though I still flinch at large birds.

Die Depression ist weg. Einfach weg. Ich kann es selbst kaum glauben. | Ich wurde mir bewusst, wie ich in Gesprächen oft nur darauf warte, selbst zu reden, statt zuzuhören. Auch in meiner Familie habe ich Muster erkannt, die sich über Generationen wiederholen, z.B. dass bei uns nie über Gefühle gesprochen wird. Das beschäftigt mich seitdem sehr. | Ich habe zum ersten Mal bewusst wahrgenommen, wie viel ich über andere urteile, und dass diese Urteile meistens mehr über mich aussagen als über die anderen. | Ich fühle mich wie neu geboren. Die Depression, die mich jahrelang begleitet hat, ist fast verschwunden. Ich kann wieder lachen, mich verlieben, Pläne machen. Ich bin so dankbar. | Ich bin seit der Erfahrung kritischer gegenüber meinem Umfeld und merke, wer es gut mit mir meint und wer nicht.

The depression is gone. Simply gone. I can hardly believe it myself. | I became aware of how, in conversations, I often just wait for my turn to talk instead of listening. I also recognised patterns in my family that repeat over generations, e.g. that we never talk about feelings. This has been on my mind a lot ever since. | For the first time I consciously noticed how much I judge others, and that these judgements usually say more about me than about the others. | I feel reborn. The depression that was with me for years has almost disappeared. I can laugh again, fall in love, make plans. I am so grateful. | Since the experience I have been more critical of the people around me, and I notice who means well with me and who does not.

    " ", "In my case the experience made stressful events harder to deal with for a long time. I had a challenging trip and afterwards developed health anxiety. Every little symptom would set off panic. It took a year of therapy to get on top of it. I'm doing better now.", 
    "Seit der Erfahrung gab es keine größeren Belastungen, daher kann ich das nicht beurteilen.", 
    " ", " ", " ", " ", " ", "I went through a period of severe stress about two years ago when my company went bankrupt and I lost everything I had invested. I was 52, with a mortgage and two kids in university. I genuinely thought about ending my life. A friend who knew about my situation suggested I try a psilocybin retreat, which he had found helpful after his own divorce. I went, expecting nothing. What I experienced was a profound sense of being held and loved. I saw my wife and children, and I felt how much they love me, regardless of money or success. I cried for hours. When I came back, I was still in a terrible financial situation, but I was no longer in despair. I talked to my wife honestly about everything, which I'd been avoiding out of shame. We made a plan together. We sold the house, moved somewhere smaller, and I found a job. We're okay now. I don't think I would have survived that period without the experience, and I'm not exaggerating.", 
    " ", " ", " ", " ", " ", "Ich bin gelassener geworden, besonders bei Kleinigkeiten, die mich früher wahnsinnig gemacht haben, wie Verspätungen der Bahn oder unfreundliche Menschen.",

    " ", "I'm a little better at it maybe. Hard to tell.", " ",

    " ", "Seit der Erfahrung gehe ich ganz anders mit Stress um. Ich war früher ein Mensch, der immer alles im Griff haben musste.     " ", " ", " ", " ", " ", "I'm more at ease with uncertainty and change. I don't need to know how everything will turn out.", 
    " ", " ", " ", " ", "I stay calmer in stressful situations and I can think more clearly, for example during exams or job interviews.", 
    " ", " ", "Ich habe durch die Erfahrung gelernt, Dinge aus einer anderen Perspektive zu betrachten.     " ", " ", "Ich bin nicht mehr so schnell gestresst und kann die Dinge leichter nehmen.",

    " ", " ", "I'm less stressed by other people's opinions of me. I used to worry so much about what everyone thought. Now I care less, in a healthy way, and that has taken a lot of pressure off.",

    " ", " ", " ", "The experience was in a ceremony with my partner, and it brought us much closer. When stressful things happen now, we face them together. ), text_acute = c("I went to a licensed psilocybin service center, which I chose specifically because I wanted it to be safe and legal. I had a preparation session with a facilitator, a calm older woman, and she was great. I wanted to work on a general sense of anxiety that I've had my whole life. I took a high dose, 35mg of psilocybin, in a comfortable room with music.<br><br>The first hour was wonderful. Colours, music that felt like it was inside me, a deep sense of relaxation. I remember thinking 'this is going to be easy'.<br><br>Then, without any warning, I couldn't breathe. It felt like there was water in my lungs. I sat up and gasped and the facilitator came over. I tried to tell her I was drowning and I couldn't get the words out. And then I was underwater. Not imagining it, being there. I was a small child, maybe three or four, and I was at the bottom of a pool looking up at the light and the shadows of people on the surface. I was kicking and nobody came. I swallowed water. My chest was burning. I knew I was going to die.<br><br>I've since learned from my mother that I nearly drowned in a hotel pool when I was three and that my uncle pulled me out. I had no conscious memory of this at all. Nobody in my family had ever mentioned it.<br><br>In the session room I apparently was gasping and clawing at my throat. The facilitator stayed calm and kept talking to me, but at some point she was worried enough about my breathing that she called the on-site supervisor, who checked my oxygen with a finger monitor. It was normal, 98 percent. They told me that. It didn't matter. In my body I was drowning and it went on and on.<br><br>Then the drowning turned into something else. I was no longer a child, I was no longer anyone. The water became a huge dark space and I was dissolving into it. It felt like the end of me, and I fought it with everything I had. The more I fought, the worse it got. The facilitator kept saying 'let it move through you', and eventually, because I had no strength left, I stopped fighting. And for a moment there was a strange quiet, like floating. That moment was peaceful. But then the panic came back in waves for the rest of the session, maybe another two hours. Each wave I was underwater again.<br><br>By the end I was lying on the floor wrapped in a blanket, completely exhausted, my throat raw from gasping. The facilitator sat with me until I could walk. My partner picked me up. I didn't speak in the car. At home I took a shower and had a panic attack when the water hit my face.<br><br>I want to say that the facilitators did everything right. This wasn't their fault. But it was the most frightening thing I've ever been through.", 
"Mushrooms, about 3g, at home with my roommate. I got stuck in a loop where I kept 'waking up' from the trip, thinking it was over, and then realising I was still in it. Each time I woke up, things were slightly different, the furniture moved, my roommate's clothes changed colour. I counted maybe 40 loops. I became convinced I'd never wake up for real, that I'd be stuck in a nested dream forever. My roommate kept telling me where I was, but each time I thought he was part of the dream.", 
"I want to start by saying that I was experienced with psychedelics, I'd done mushrooms maybe 15 times, and I thought I knew what I was doing. That arrogance is part of the story.<br><br>It was October and I decided to go on a solo hike in a national park and take a large dose of mushrooms, around 5 grams, at a spot I'd been to before, a viewpoint about two hours' walk from the car park. My plan was to sit there for the peak and walk back in the afternoon. I told nobody where I was going. My father had died that summer and I wanted to 'connect' with him and with nature.<br><br>I took the mushrooms around 11am. The come-up was very fast and strong. Within 40 minutes I couldn't stand properly. The landscape started to breathe and pulse, and the trees looked like they were made of light. For a while it was overwhelming but beautiful. Then I saw my father. Not like a hallucination exactly, but I knew he was there, sitting on a rock nearby. He looked sick, the way he looked in the hospital at the end. He didn't say anything. He just looked at me with this terrible sadness. I started to cry and I tried to go to him and I fell down a small slope and hurt my ankle.<br><br>After that, everything turned. The light was going (I didn't realise how late it was, I'd lost all sense of time), and the trees around me became threatening. I heard voices in the wind, and I felt that the forest was angry that I was there. I started to believe I was going to die there, that my father had come to take me with him. Then I lost the sense of being a person at all. I was just fear, spread across the whole forest. I don't know how long this lasted.<br><br>When I became somewhat aware again it was dark. I was cold, my ankle was swollen and I was still tripping. My phone had almost no battery and no signal. I tried to walk back but I couldn't find the trail. I kept hearing things moving in the bushes, and every shadow looked like a figure. I sat down under a tree and wrapped myself in my rain jacket and shook all night. I was convinced I would freeze to death, and part of me thought I deserved it for not being there more for my dad.<br><br>At first light I started walking and eventually found a forest road. A ranger in a truck picked me up around 9am. I was hypothermic and had a sprained ankle, and I spent a night in a small hospital. The doctors were kind, but I was too ashamed to tell them about the mushrooms at first. When I finally told my sister what had happened, she cried and said she could have lost two family members in one year.", 
"High dose of LSD alone. I became convinced I was in hell and that I'd been there forever. My life before was a memory implanted to make the torment worse. I lay on my floor for 8 hours seeing flames.", 
"Ich habe auf einer Silvesterparty LSD genommen. Um Mitternacht ging das Feuerwerk los, und es war fuer mich wie ein Bombenangriff. Ich habe mich auf den Boden geworfen und die Haende ueber den Kopf gelegt. Jeder Knall war eine Explosion, jedes Licht ein Einschlag. Meine Freunde haben gelacht, weil sie dachten, ich mache Spass, bis sie gesehen haben, dass ich weine. Ich habe mich in der Wohnung im Bad eingeschlossen und bin bis zum Morgen nicht herausgekommen.", 
"Viel zu hoch dosiertes LSD. Ich habe mich selbst voellig verloren und dachte, ich bin fuer immer verrueckt.", 
"Ich hatte im Studentenwohnheim allein Pilze genommen und war in einer sehr duesteren Stimmung. Ich habe laut geweint und geschrien, weil ich das Gefuehl hatte, dass mein Leben sinnlos ist. Meine Mitbewohnerin hat das gehoert und gedacht, ich will mir etwas antun. Sie hat einen Krankenwagen gerufen, und mit dem Krankenwagen kam die Polizei. Ich war mitten im Trip, als ploetzlich fremde Menschen in Uniform in meinem Zimmer standen und mich gefragt haben, ob ich mich umbringen will. Ich konnte nicht erklaeren, was los war. Ich habe nur geweint. Sie haben mich mitgenommen, in die Psychiatrie, und ich musste die Nacht dort verbringen. Das Zimmer war kahl, mit einem Fenster aus Milchglas und einer Tuer ohne Klinke. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, fuer immer eingesperrt zu sein. Am naechsten Morgen hat eine Aerztin mit mir gesprochen und mich entlassen, nachdem sie verstanden hatte, dass es die Pilze waren.", 
"I took a high dose of 1P-LSD, maybe 250-300ug, by myself on a Saturday and decided to walk around the city because I thought it would be interesting. For a while it was. Then I went down into the subway because the noise outside was too much, and it was a terrible decision. The fluorescent lights were flickering and everyone on the platform looked like they were made of plastic, with blank, identical faces. I became convinced that everyone around me was a robot, that I was the last real human being, and that if they found out I was human they'd do something to me. I got on a train just to get away and rode it to the end of the line.<br><br>When I got out I was in a part of the city I didn't know at all. My phone battery was dead. It was getting dark. I was walking around for hours, trying to find my way back, and every street looked the same. I was crying and talking to myself. People were crossing the street to avoid me. At one point I sat down on a bench and a homeless man sat next to me and asked if I was alright. I told him that everyone was robots and he laughed in a kind way and said 'yeah, sometimes it feels like that'. He stayed with me for a long time and shared his tea from a thermos. He told me about his life. Eventually he walked me to a bus stop and told me which bus to take. I don't know his name. I think about him a lot.", 
"I'd followed an online wellness influencer who sold a course about 'healing your inner child with a heroic dose'. The course said that 5g of dried mushrooms alone in silent darkness was the way to break through trauma. I followed the instructions exactly. I'd been bullied badly at school and I thought this would heal it.<br><br>What happened was that I relived the bullying. Not remembered, relived. I was 12 again in the school toilets, with the older boys holding my head down. I could smell the bleach, hear their laughter. Then it got worse, because the trip added things: the boys' faces became demonic, their laughter became a roar, and I was not just in the toilets but in some kind of hell made of toilets, endless rows, and every one had a boy laughing at me.<br><br>I tried to tell myself it was the mushrooms, but that thought kept slipping away. I became convinced I deserved all of it, that I was worthless and disgusting, that everyone who'd ever met me had secretly despised me. I curled up on the floor and hit myself in the face, which I hadn't done since school.<br><br>When it ended, eight hours later, I lay there exhausted with a bruised cheek. The course had a section called 'integration' which said to journal about your breakthrough. I didn't have a breakthrough. I had the worst night of my life.", 
"I want to describe this carefully because I've never read about anyone having exactly this experience.<br><br>I booked a 'dark retreat': seven days in total darkness in a small hut in the mountains, with food passed in through a light-tight hatch. The idea, according to the organisers, is that after a few days in the dark the brain begins to produce its own psychedelic states. On top of that, they offered an optional 'plant medicine' on day four, which turned out to be a brew containing harmala alkaloids and DMT-containing bark, an ayahuasca analogue. I'd done ayahuasca twice before with good experiences and I wanted to go deeper. I signed the waiver.<br><br>Days one to three were hard but manageable. I lost track of time quickly. I slept and woke at random. I meditated. I began to see coloured lights and shapes, which the organiser said was normal. By day three I was having vivid waking dreams. I heard voices sometimes, mostly my own thoughts, but very loud. I was lonely but also curious.<br><br>On day four the brew was passed through the hatch with a small candle, which I was told to blow out after drinking. I drank it and sat in the darkness.<br><br>What followed I can only describe as the darkness coming alive. Without any light, the visions had nothing to anchor to. They filled the whole space. I saw the walls of the hut covered in eyes, thousands of them, opening one by one. I heard breathing that wasn't mine. Something sat down next to me on the mattress. I felt the mattress dip. I reached out and there was nothing there, but I felt it lean against me.<br><br>Then I lost my body. In the darkness there was no way to check where my hands were, no way to see myself. I felt I had become the darkness itself, an infinite black space, and that there was no hut, no mountain, no world. I had always existed in the dark and the light was the dream. I kept trying to remember a single image from my life, my mother's kitchen, my partner's face, and each time the image was swallowed as soon as it formed.<br><br>I don't know how long this lasted. In the dark there's no time. It could have been an hour or twelve. At some point I started screaming, and I realised that nobody could hear me. The hut was far from the main house. The protocol was that you knock three times on the hatch in an emergency. I couldn't find the hatch. I crawled along the walls feeling for it, and the walls seemed to go on forever, corners kept appearing where there shouldn't be corners. I was convinced I was trapped in an infinite maze in the dark, and that I'd die there.<br><br>Eventually I found the hatch and knocked. Nothing happened. I knocked again and again until my knuckles bled. I don't know how long it took, but eventually it opened and light came in, just a sliver, and it was like being hit by lightning. The organiser's voice asked if I wanted to end the retreat. I said yes. He said it might be better to 'stay with the process' until morning. I begged. He said he would come back in an hour. He closed the hatch.<br><br>That hour was the worst of my life. I sat by the hatch with my hand on it, rocking back and forth, feeling the presence next to me, hearing it breathe.<br><br>When he came back he opened the door. The light was blinding. He led me out with a blindfold, because coming into full light suddenly can be harmful, he said. I spent the rest of the day in a room with dim light, alone, still tripping. Every shadow moved. I left the next morning.",

"Ich war mit Freunden auf einem Festival und wir hatten Pilze genommen. Ploetzlich hat eine Freundin angefangen zu krampfen. Ich wusste nicht, ob das echt ist oder ob ich halluziniere. "This happened when I was 26, and I'm 31 now. I'll try to describe it as fully as I can, because I've only ever told pieces of it.<br><br>I was living in a shared house with four other people. One of my housemates, I'll call her R, was into psychedelics and spirituality, and she was organising a 'full moon ceremony' in the garden with some friends from her meditation group. She invited me. There would be mushroom tea and a fire. I'd only done mushrooms once before, a small amount at a festival, and I liked it. I said yes.<br><br>There were about eight of us around the fire. R made the tea in a big pot and served it in mugs. I didn't know how much was in each mug. In hindsight, I think the tea was very strong and the dosing very uneven. The first hour was lovely. We sang some songs R had taught us. The fire crackled. The moon came up over the neighbours' roofs, enormous and orange.<br><br>Then, gradually, I noticed that I couldn't follow the songs anymore. The words lost their meaning. The faces around the fire started to look like masks, flickering in the firelight, and behind each mask I sensed something else, something not human. The fire became a mouth. The moon became an eye. I felt a huge, cold attention focus on me, the same way you might focus on an insect.<br><br>I tried to say something to R, but my voice sounded wrong, deep and slow, like a recording played at the wrong speed. She smiled at me and said 'let it come'. I don't think she realised how bad it was. I started to lose the sense of where my body ended. My hands were part of the grass. My breathing was the wind. I felt myself spreading out over the garden, thinner and thinner, until there was hardly anything left. And then there was a moment, I can't say how long, when there was nothing at all. No me, no garden, no moon. Just a black, silent, infinite absence.<br><br>When I came back from that, I was in total panic. I didn't know who I was or what I was. I knew there had been a 'before', but I couldn't remember it. I had a body but didn't know how to use it. I tried to stand and fell into the flower bed. Someone helped me up and I screamed at them, because their face was a mask with nothing behind it.<br><br>I ran into the house. Inside, under the electric light, everything was even worse. The kitchen looked like a hospital, sterile and threatening. The fridge was humming a threatening note. I went to my room and locked the door. I sat on my bed and tried to remember my name. I found my wallet and looked at my ID card. The name meant nothing. The face in the photo meant nothing. I remember looking at it and thinking: this is a stranger, and I've stolen his life.<br><br>I don't know how long I sat there. At some point R knocked and asked if I was okay. I didn't answer. She went away. Later, another housemate who hadn't taken anything, I'll call him T, knocked and said he was worried, and asked if he could come in. I opened the door because his voice sounded normal. He sat with me on the floor. He didn't try to explain anything. He just talked about ordinary things: the football results, a film he'd seen, what he was going to cook tomorrow. I didn't understand most of it, but the ordinariness was like a rope. He stayed with me until it was light.<br><br>When the sun came up I knew my name again. But the feeling that it was someone else's name, that I was living in a stolen life, didn't go away with the drug. That feeling has been with me, on and off, ever since.<br><br>The next day R came to my room with a cup of tea and said it sounded like I'd had a 'beautiful ego death'. I asked her to leave. I moved out two months later.", 
"DMT. Saw god and god was furious with me. I was terrified for maybe 10 minutes.", 
"I'm a researcher and I volunteered for a phase 1 study of extended-state DMT, where DMT is given by continuous infusion so the experience lasts much longer than when you smoke it. I was screened, prepared, and I'd had experience with psychedelics before. I felt I was in the safest possible setting. I want to be clear that the study team was professional throughout.<br><br>The infusion started and within a minute I was gone. It was like being shot out of a cannon into another world. At first it was astonishing. Architectures of light, intelligences that seemed to welcome me. I remember thinking 'this is the most important moment of my life'.<br><br>But in a normal DMT experience you come back after 10-15 minutes. Here, I didn't come back. The world kept going. After what felt like a very long time, I began to lose track of the fact that I had a body or a life outside this place. The beings began to treat me as if I belonged there. One of them said, without words, that I had always been there, that the human life had been a short dream. And I believed it. I couldn't remember what 'human' meant.<br><br>Then a very deep terror set in. Not of the beings, but of the realisation that I would never wake up. That there was no 'outside'. That I had dissolved into this and there was nothing to go back to. I tried to remember my wife's face and couldn't. I tried to remember my name. There was nothing. Just an infinity of shifting patterns and a total absence of self. I wanted to scream but I had no mouth. The study protocol had a hand signal to stop the infusion, and I couldn't remember that I had hands.<br><br>The infusion lasted about 90 minutes in clock time. The study staff told me later that my vital signs were stable but that at some point my face showed visible distress, and they discussed stopping, but because I didn't give the signal and the protocol allowed for difficult experiences, they continued. I don't blame them.<br><br>When the infusion stopped and I came back, it was not a relief at first. It was like falling into a body that wasn't mine. The room, the researchers, the bed, all looked like a crude set. I didn't believe they were real. One of the researchers said my name and it sounded like a foreign word. It took about 30 minutes before I could speak coherently and maybe an hour before I felt like I was 'in' my life again. Even then I wasn't fully sure.<br><br>I did the post-session interview, and I tried to describe what happened, but I don't think I conveyed the horror of it. I went home that evening. My wife picked me up and I looked at her for a long time trying to decide if she was real.", 
"Ich hatte bei Freunden Pilze genommen. Irgendwann war ich ueberzeugt, dass alle meine Gedanken laut hoerbar sind und dass alle wissen, was ich denke. Ich habe mich furchtbar geschaemt und mich in eine Ecke gesetzt.", 
"Ketamin auf einer Party, viel zu viel. Ich war im K-Loch und hatte das Gefuehl, tot zu sein und nie mehr zurueckzukommen.", 
"I was 16 and my older cousin, who was 20, gave me LSD at a family barbecue at his parents' place. He said it would be fun and that he'd look after me. I'd never taken anything before except a bit of weed. For the first hour I felt giggly and the colours were nice. Then my aunt called everyone to the table and I had to sit there with the whole family, my parents, my grandparents, my little sister. The food started to move on the plate. The meat looked alive. My grandfather's face kept changing, sometimes old, sometimes young, sometimes like a skull. I couldn't follow the conversation, people were asking me questions about school and I didn't know how to answer.<br><br>I became terrified that my parents would find out. Then I became terrified that I'd broken my brain and would be like this forever, and that my life was over at 16. I went to the bathroom and locked the door and looked in the mirror and didn't recognise my own face. My cousin came and knocked and told me to come out and act normal. He sounded annoyed, not worried. I didn't come out for an hour. My mum knocked and asked if I was sick and I said I had a stomach ache.<br><br>We went home and I lay in my bed all night with my eyes open, watching the ceiling crawl, sure that I was going insane. I had school the next morning and I went because I was afraid that staying home would make my parents suspicious. I sat through classes still feeling strange, everything too loud and too bright. I didn't tell anyone for years.", 
"My partner and I had been together for six years. We decided to take mushrooms together on a weekend away to celebrate our anniversary. It was meant to be romantic. About two hours in, we were lying in the grass by a river, holding hands, and he started crying. I thought it was a happy cry. Then he said there was something he had to tell me, that the mushrooms were showing him he couldn't hide it anymore. He told me he had been seeing someone else for eight months.<br><br>I don't think there's a worse place to hear that than at the peak of a mushroom trip. The world split in two. The river turned grey and the trees turned their backs on me. I felt like my entire life with him had been a film that had suddenly been revealed as fake, and that the 'real' world was cold and empty. I looked at his face and it kept changing, sometimes the man I loved, sometimes a stranger, sometimes something reptilian and cold.<br><br>I couldn't get away, we were in the middle of nowhere and neither of us could drive. I walked along the river for hours, crying and screaming at the sky. I felt like I was disintegrating. He followed me at a distance, crying too. I hated him for following me, and I was also terrified to be alone.<br><br>When the drug wore off we sat in the cottage in silence until morning. Then he drove us home and I moved out the next week.", 
"Took LSD at home, got stuck in a thought loop about whether I'd locked the door. Checked it maybe 200 times. Each time I wasn't sure if I'd really checked. Exhausting and horrible.", 
"I am a gay man from a country where homosexuality is not accepted, and where drug use is punished harshly. I'll leave the country unnamed. At the time of this experience I was living in the capital, very much in the closet at work and with my family. My boyfriend and I had a small apartment that we said we shared as 'friends'.<br><br>A friend who'd lived in Europe brought back some LSD and gave us two tabs. We waited for a weekend when we had nothing planned and took them at home. For a few hours it was the most beautiful experience. We felt free, we danced, we laughed, we held each other. For the first time in my life I felt completely accepted as I am.<br><br>Then, in the evening, we heard loud banging on the door. Police. Later I found out that our neighbour had heard music and two men's voices, and had been suspicious of us for a long time. I was at the peak of the trip. The banging sounded like the end of the world. My boyfriend tried to hide the remaining tabs. I opened the door because I thought that if I didn't, they would break it.<br><br>Four officers came in. They saw how we looked, our pupils, and they knew immediately. They searched the apartment and found the foil with the tabs. They found photos on my phone of me and my boyfriend. One of them started shouting the word they use for gay men, and hit my boyfriend in the face. I froze. The colours were still moving, the officers' faces were melting and turning into animal faces. I didn't know if this was real or if I had gone insane.<br><br>They handcuffed us and took us to the police station in separate cars. I sat in the back of the car and watched the city lights stream past like rivers of blood. In the station they put me in a small room with one bare bulb. The bulb was pulsing. I was alone for what felt like days. Then two officers came in and interrogated me. They wanted names: who gave us the drugs, who else was gay, who else was in our circle. When I didn't answer, one of them slapped me repeatedly. They threatened to call my family and my employer. They said I would go to prison for years and that I'd be raped there. I was still tripping and I believed everything they said, more than believed, I saw it happening.<br><br>At some point I lost myself completely. There was no more me, just fear and the bulb and the voices. I think I gave them some names. I don't remember. That's one of the things I can't forgive myself for.<br><br>We were held for two days. My boyfriend had a broken nose. A cousin of mine who is a lawyer got us out. I don't know what he paid. My family found out about everything. My father didn't speak to me for a year.<br><br>Three months later, my boyfriend and I left the country. We applied for asylum in Europe. That's where I'm living now.", 
"Ich war in einer schweren Krise nach dem Tod meiner Frau und habe zum ersten Mal Psilocybin genommen, allein in unserem Haus. Ich hatte gehofft, sie zu spueren. Stattdessen habe ich die letzten Wochen ihres Lebens noch einmal erlebt, im Krankenhaus, ihr Gesicht, wie sie keine Luft mehr bekommt, das Piepen der Geraete. Ich war wieder dort, mit allen Gefuehlen der Hilflosigkeit. Dann hat sich das Haus verwandelt. Jeder Gegenstand, ihre Brille, ihre Gartenhandschuhe, ihre Buecher, wurde zu einem Vorwurf. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass ich sie im Stich gelassen habe, dass ich mehr haette tun muessen. Ich habe stundenlang auf ihrem Sessel gesessen, mich nicht bewegen koennen und mit ihr geredet, ohne dass sie geantwortet hat. Irgendwann habe ich gedacht, dass ich ihr folgen sollte. Ich habe meine Tochter angerufen, mitten in der Nacht, und sie ist sofort gekommen. Ohne sie weiss ich nicht, was passiert waere.", 
"At a retreat in Peru I was offered kambo (frog poison) in the morning before an ayahuasca ceremony in the evening. Nobody explained the risks properly. The kambo made me vomit and my face swelled up and I felt like I was suffocating. My heart was racing and I lay on the ground for an hour unable to move. I was still weak in the evening but they said the ceremony would 'complete the cleansing'. The ayahuasca hit me very hard because I was dehydrated and exhausted. I saw myself as a corpse being eaten by insects. I couldn't get up to go to the toilet and soiled myself. I felt utterly humiliated and terrified. Nobody came to help me until morning.", 
"Smoked DMT. The entities told me I'd been there before and that I'd forgotten on purpose because what I'd learned was too terrible. Then they showed me. I can't describe it. Something about the nature of suffering and that it never ends. Came back sobbing.", 
"Someone passed me a DMT vape at a house party and I took a big hit without really knowing what it was. I broke through and found myself in a room made of shifting machinery. There were small beings, bouncing and chattering, and they showed me that the world I came from was a simulation they had built. They laughed at me for believing it was real. Then they turned me inside out. I could see the code behind everything, and my own life was just a loop running in that code. When I came back to the party, I didn't believe anyone was real. I looked at my friends and they seemed like NPCs. I left and walked home alone, trying to find a glitch that would prove it.", 
"I have a family history of schizophrenia, my uncle. I knew it was risky but I was 19 and felt invincible. I took a moderate dose of LSD at a friend's place. A couple of hours in, I started to hear voices. Not the usual auditory distortions, but distinct voices, talking about me in the third person, commenting on what I was doing. They were critical and nasty. I realised what was happening and that made me panic, I was sure I'd triggered the same illness as my uncle. The voices got louder and started arguing with each other about whether I deserved to live. I covered my ears and rocked back and forth on the floor.", 
"LSD mit Freunden, schoener Abend, bis ich ploetzlich ueberzeugt war, dass meine Mutter gestorben ist. Ich habe sie mitten in der Nacht angerufen und geweint. Sie war natuerlich voellig verwirrt und erschrocken.", 
"Ich habe zum ersten Mal Psilocybin genommen, in einer legalen Sitzung in den Niederlanden. Die Begleiterin war freundlich, die Umgebung schoen. Trotzdem hatte ich eine sehr schwierige Erfahrung. Ich habe gespuert, wie ich mich selbst verliere, und hatte das Gefuehl, verrueckt zu werden. Ich habe mich an der Hand der Begleiterin festgehalten, bis es vorbei war. Am Ende hatte ich einen kurzen Moment grosser Klarheit.", 
"Ich habe mit 16 auf einer Klassenfahrt zum ersten Mal Pilze genommen. Ein Mitschueler hatte sie besorgt. Ich bin mit zwei anderen in den Wald gegangen. Nach einer Stunde hatte ich das Gefuehl, dass die Baeume mich festhalten wollen. Ich habe mich verlaufen und bin stundenlang durch den Wald geirrt. Die Lehrer haben eine Suchaktion gestartet, und ich wurde schliesslich von der Polizei gefunden, nachts, zitternd und voellig verwirrt. Danach gab es riesigen Aerger, mit der Schule, mit meinen Eltern und mit der Polizei.", 
"Smoked salvia and felt like I was being pulled into a giant zipper in the fabric of reality. Lasted 3 minutes but felt eternal.", 
"I took 4-HO-MET with a friend at his place. It's supposed to be a light, visual psychedelic. But after the peak I got very restless and couldn't stop moving. Then I became sure that there were insects under my skin. I could feel them crawling. I scratched my arms until they bled. My friend tried to stop me, and I thought he was putting more insects on me. That lasted about three hours. The next morning my arms looked like I'd fought a cat.", 
"Ich habe mit meiner besten Freundin LSD genommen, und sie hat einen sehr schlechten Trip bekommen. Sie hat geschrien, sich die Haare ausgerissen und wollte aus dem Fenster im vierten Stock steigen. Ich habe sie festgehalten und war selbst mitten im Trip. Ihr Gesicht hat sich staendig veraendert, und ich hatte panische Angst, dass sie springt oder dass ich sie nicht halten kann. Ich habe mit einer Hand den Notruf gewaehlt. Die Sanitaeter und die Polizei kamen, und sie wurde mitgenommen. Ich sass danach allein in der Wohnung und konnte nicht aufhoeren zu zittern.", 
"Ich habe LSD genommen und hatte ploetzlich das Gefuehl, dass meine verstorbenen Grosseltern im Raum sind. Am Anfang war das schoen, ich habe mich gefreut, sie zu sehen. Dann haben sie angefangen, mich anzuklagen. Sie haben mir vorgeworfen, dass ich sie im Altenheim kaum besucht habe, dass ich bei ihrer Beerdigung nicht geweint habe, dass ich ein schlechter Enkel bin. Ihre Stimmen wurden immer lauter, und ihre Gesichter wurden grau und eingefallen, so wie bei der Aufbahrung. Ich habe mich entschuldigt, immer wieder, aber sie haben nicht aufgehoert. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, vor einem Gericht zu stehen. Irgendwann bin ich aus der Wohnung gerannt und habe mich in den Hausflur gesetzt, weil ich dachte, dass sie mir dort nicht folgen koennen. Ich sass dort stundenlang im Dunkeln und habe geweint, bis ein Nachbar mich gefunden und gefragt hat, ob er jemanden anrufen soll.", 
"Ich habe als Medizinstudentin an einem Wochenende mit Freunden LSD genommen und mich dabei in eine Gedankenspirale ueber Krankheiten verstrickt. Ich war ploetzlich ueberzeugt, dass ich einen Hirntumor habe, dass ich die Symptome schon lange ignoriert habe und dass ich bald sterben werde. Ich habe alle Symptome, die ich je gelernt habe, an mir gespuert: Kopfschmerzen, Sehstoerungen, Taubheit in den Haenden. Ich habe meinen Freunden erklaert, dass ich sofort ins Krankenhaus muss, und sie haben mich davon abgehalten, was ich ihnen damals furchtbar uebel genommen habe. Ich lag die ganze Nacht wach und habe meinen Koerper abgetastet und bin innerlich meine Beerdigung durchgegangen.", 
"Smoked salvia at a party. For maybe 5 minutes I became a chair in a kitchen in another world. I forgot I was ever human. When I came back I was terrified that I would be a chair again. Short but horrible.", 
"I did a 'hippie flip' (mushrooms then MDMA) at a friend's flat. It went fine until my friends thought it'd be funny to tell me I'd been tripping for three days and that they'd been taking care of me. I believed them completely. I thought I'd lost three days of my life and that my brain was broken. I panicked, cried, tried to call my parents. They told me it was a joke an hour later but I couldn't shake the feeling.", 
"Ich mache seit einer Weile Microdosing mit Pilzen. An einem Morgen habe ich offenbar die Kapseln verwechselt und eine viel zu hohe Dosis genommen, bevor ich ins Buero gefahren bin. Nach einer Stunde im Meeting merkte ich, dass etwas nicht stimmt. Die Gesichter meiner Kollegen begannen sich zu verziehen, und ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass alle wissen, was los ist, und mich beobachten. Ich habe mich auf der Toilette eingeschlossen und gewartet, bis es vorbei ist. Ich hatte panische Angst, dass jemand es merkt und ich meinen Job verliere.", 
"A friend obtained synthetic mescaline and we took it at his house in the countryside. Nobody told us how long it lasts. The come-up was slow, two hours of nausea and restlessness. Then it hit hard and just kept going. Hour after hour. By the 10th hour I was desperate for it to end and it didn't. The sun went down and came back up, or at least I thought it did, and I was still tripping.<br><br>Somewhere in the night I became delirious. I couldn't tell what time it was or how long I'd been there. I had conversations with people who weren't in the room. I thought I was in a hospital and that the doctors were keeping me in this state on purpose. I couldn't sleep, though I was beyond exhausted. My body felt like it was buzzing with electricity and my jaw ached from clenching.<br><br>By the 14th hour I started believing that it would never end, that I had permanently altered my brain chemistry and that I'd be like this for the rest of my life. That was the worst fear. My friend was in a similar state and couldn't help me. I finally slept a little the next afternoon, and when I woke up the world still looked wrong for several more days.", 
"Ich habe als Studentin bei einem Besuch in meinem Elternhaus mit meinem Bruder Pilze genommen, als unsere Eltern eigentlich uebers Wochenende weg sein sollten. Mein Vater hat frueher viel getrunken und war dann oft gewalttaetig, vor allem gegenueber meiner Mutter. Inzwischen ist er trocken, aber die Erinnerungen sind geblieben.<br><br>Mitten im Trip hoerten wir den Schluessel in der Tuer. Mein Vater kam frueher zurueck, allein, weil er sich mit meiner Mutter gestritten hatte. Er war nicht betrunken, aber er war wuetend und laut. In dem Moment, als ich seine Stimme im Flur hoerte, war ich wieder acht Jahre alt. Ich habe mich in meinem alten Kinderzimmer unter der Bettdecke versteckt, genau wie damals. Ich hoerte durch die Wand das Geschrei von frueher, das Klirren von Glaesern, meine Mutter, die weint. Ich wusste nicht mehr, was jetzt passiert und was damals passiert ist.<br><br>Mein Bruder hat versucht, mit meinem Vater zu reden und ihn abzulenken, aber auch er war voellig verwirrt. Ich habe stundenlang unter der Decke gelegen und mich nicht bewegt, aus Angst, dass er reinkommt. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, mein ganzes erwachsenes Leben sei nur ein Traum gewesen und ich sei immer noch das kleine Maedchen in diesem Haus. Als ich am naechsten Morgen aufgewacht bin, hat mein Vater Fruehstueck gemacht und so getan, als sei nichts gewesen. Fuer ihn war ja auch nichts gewesen.", 
"I was on mushrooms at a friend's place when I got a text from my bank saying that my account had been emptied by fraud. I'd just been paid that day. In a normal state, I'd have called the bank. On mushrooms, I spiralled. I became convinced it was a sign that my whole life was collapsing, that I would lose my flat, my job, that I'd end up homeless. I saw myself sleeping in a doorway in winter, old and alone. I couldn't use my phone properly, the bank's app was a mess of moving symbols. I walked around the garden in circles for hours, crying and talking to myself. My friend tried to help but I couldn't hear anything. The next day I called the bank and they returned all the money within a week.", 
"I was a child refugee from the war in the Balkans. I came to Germany at seven. I'd done years of therapy and thought I had dealt with it. I did an MDMA-assisted session with a therapist who works underground, because legal options didn't exist where I live. The MDMA made me feel safe and open, and we talked about my childhood. Then, unexpectedly, I was back in the basement in my hometown where we hid during the shelling. I could hear the explosions, smell the damp concrete and the fear of the adults. I saw my mother's face lit by a candle, trying to smile at me. I was seven again and terrified. I started shaking and crying and crawled under the therapist's desk, which felt like the basement. She stayed calm and sat on the floor next to me and talked to me in a soft voice for a long time. I sobbed like I had never sobbed before. At some point, I came out from under the desk and she hugged me. It was terrifying and yet also something I had needed for thirty years.", 
"Wir waren auf einem Festival, als in der Nacht ein heftiges Unwetter kam. Ich hatte LSD genommen und lag im Zelt, als der Sturm das Zelt eingerissen hat. Ploetzlich war alles nass, kalt und laut, der Boden war ein einziger Schlammsee. Ich konnte im Dunkeln nichts sehen und habe den Ausgang nicht gefunden. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, im Schlamm zu ertrinken, und habe um mich geschlagen. Ueberall um mich herum haben Menschen geschrien, und der Donner war so laut, dass ich dachte, die Welt geht unter. Ich habe mich an einen Pfosten geklammert und bin bis zum Morgen nicht losgekommen. Ich habe meine Freunde erst am naechsten Mittag wiedergefunden.", 
"I'm a gay man and I went to a private party where people were taking 2C-B. I'd done it once before at a club and liked it. At this party the host gave me a dose that was much stronger than I expected. It came on fast and I became very disoriented and floppy, I could barely stand. The lights were spinning and the music was a wall of noise.<br><br>Some men started touching me. At first I wasn't sure if it was happening or if I was imagining it, everything felt unreal and liquid. I tried to say no, I think I did say no, but my words came out slurred and quiet. I couldn't move my arms properly. I felt like I was underwater and they were on the surface. My sense of my own body dissolved. I was a body on a couch and I was also floating somewhere near the ceiling, watching.<br><br>I don't know exactly what happened. I have fragments. Hands. A laugh. Someone saying 'he's fine, he's into it'. I wasn't into it. I was frozen.<br><br>At some point I was alone in a bathroom, sitting in the dry bathtub. I don't know how I got there. I stayed there for a long time, shaking, until the drug started to wear off. Then I found my clothes and my phone and left. It was 6am. I walked home through empty streets feeling like I had been erased.", 
"Ich bin auf Pilzen joggen gegangen, weil ich dachte, das waere ein tolles Naturerlebnis. Nach ein paar Kilometern hatte ich das Gefuehl, dass mein Herz aussetzt. Ich habe gespuert, wie es stolpert, dann ganz schnell schlaegt, dann wieder stolpert. Ich bin stehen geblieben und habe mich an einen Baum gelehnt. Der Wald hat sich um mich gedreht. Ich war allein, weit weg von der Strasse, und hatte panische Angst, dass ich hier an einem Herzstillstand sterbe und niemand mich findet. Ich habe mich hingesetzt und eine Ewigkeit lang meinen Puls gezaehlt, bis ich mich getraut habe, langsam zurueckzugehen.", 
"I grew up in a very strict religious family. By my twenties I'd left the church, but a lot of the beliefs were still in me somewhere, I just didn't know it. I took LSD with a couple of friends at my apartment. It was my third time.<br><br>About two hours in, I started to feel something inside my chest. A presence. At first it felt like warmth, then it turned cold and heavy. I suddenly 'knew' that this was a demon, that by taking drugs I had opened a door, and that the demon had come in. Every warning my mother had ever given me came rushing back. I felt it moving inside me, taking over my arms, my voice. When I tried to speak it came out in a deep, strange voice, or that's how it sounded to me. My friends were scared, which made me more convinced that they could see the demon too.<br><br>I started praying, out loud, the old prayers from my childhood. I hadn't said them in years. I begged God to forgive me. I felt the demon laughing inside me. I saw its face in the mirror instead of mine, grey and twisted. I scratched at my arms trying to get it out, I drew blood. My friends tried to stop me and I fought them off.<br><br>One of my friends, in a panic, called my mother because he didn't know what else to do. That was a mistake, though I understand why he did it. My mother and father arrived about an hour later with the pastor from their church. They saw me bleeding and screaming and praying, and they believed exactly what I believed. The pastor put his hands on my head and started a deliverance prayer, which is like an exorcism. My parents held my arms. They were shouting at the demon to leave me, commanding it in the name of Jesus. This went on for a long time, at least an hour. I was terrified, I was in agony, and I was being held down by my parents while a man shouted at the thing inside me.<br><br>At some point I collapsed and they took that as the demon leaving. My mother cried and hugged me and said I was saved. I was still tripping and still felt the presence, just weaker. They took me home with them and I spent the next three days at my parents' house, being prayed over, made to read scripture, not allowed to be alone. I didn't know how to tell them it was the drug. I wasn't sure myself.<br><br>Eventually I went back to my apartment. My friends were shaken and we never talked about it properly. I didn't tell my parents about the LSD until two years later.", 
"A group of four of us went to the desert in Arizona to take peyote buttons that one of my friends had been given by someone. It was summer, which in hindsight was idiotic. We started in the late morning. The taste was horrible and I threw up twice in the first hour, which I had been told was normal. By noon it was over 40 degrees and there was almost no shade. I started to feel the peyote but also the heat, and they became the same thing. My skin was burning, my head was pounding, and I felt like the sun was a giant eye staring into me.<br>I lost track of my friends. I think I wandered off to find shade. I sat under a rock overhang and the rock started to breathe. I saw faces in the rock, old faces, and I felt that they were my ancestors and that they were telling me it was time to come with them. I believed I was dying, and part of me accepted it. I remember thinking that this was a peaceful way to go. But then my body panicked, my heart was beating so fast I could feel it in my eyes, and I couldn't get enough air. I tried to stand and fell.<br>My friends found me about two hours later. One of them had water and they poured it over me and made me drink. They had to half-carry me back to the car and then drive two hours to a town with a clinic. I was diagnosed with heat exhaustion and severe dehydration. I was lucky.", 
"Ich bin Krankenschwester und habe in meiner Freizeit Pilze genommen, an einem Wochenende allein zu Hause. Waehrend des Trips musste ich an eine Patientin denken, die in meiner Schicht gestorben war, eine junge Mutter. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass sie im Raum ist und mich anschaut, mit vorwurfsvollen Augen. Ich habe mich gefragt, ob ich etwas uebersehen habe, ob ich schuld bin. Das Gefuehl wurde immer staerker, bis ich das Gefuehl hatte, dass alle Patienten, die je auf meiner Station gestorben sind, im Raum stehen. Ich habe mich unter der Bettdecke versteckt und stundenlang geweint. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass ich das nie wieder loswerde.", 
"Ich habe in den Niederlanden an einer Ayahuasca-Zeremonie teilgenommen, eigentlich um meine Depression zu behandeln. Nach dem zweiten Becher musste ich mich heftig uebergeben, und dann kamen Bilder, die ich nicht erwartet hatte. Ich sah mich als kleines Kind im Haus meines Onkels, und ploetzlich waren da Erinnerungen an Dinge, die er mit mir gemacht hat. Ich hatte das vollkommen vergessen, oder verdraengt. Es war, als wuerde ich es noch einmal erleben, mit allen Gefuehlen und Geruechen. Ich habe geschrien und mich zusammengerollt. Die Leiterin der Zeremonie hat mich gehalten, aber ich konnte nicht unterscheiden, ob sie es ist oder er. Ich wollte, dass es aufhoert, aber es hoerte nicht auf.", 
"I booked a float tank session and decided, stupidly, to take a moderate dose of mushrooms beforehand. In the tank, in total darkness and silence, floating in body-temperature water, I lost all sense of where my body was. Very quickly I didn't know if I had a body at all. I felt that I'd dissolved into the water and that the water was infinite. I couldn't find the walls of the tank. I panicked and splashed and got salt water in my eyes, which burned terribly. I couldn't find the door or the light switch. I was sure I was drowning in an endless black sea. I started screaming. The staff came after a few minutes and opened the tank. The light was blinding. I was shaking and crying and couldn't explain what was wrong. They sat with me in the lobby until I could leave.", 
"I was in my first year at college and took LSD in my dorm with my roommate and a few people from our floor. I'd never done it before. A couple of hours in, I got very emotional and started crying about my parents' divorce, and then I started talking to the wall, because I thought it was alive and was listening to me. I was saying very personal things, about my dad, about being lonely, about a girl I liked. I didn't realise that one of the guys was filming me on his phone.<br><br>Later in the trip I became very paranoid. I thought everyone was laughing at me, and I was right, they were. I saw them looking at the phone and giggling. I asked what they were watching and they hid it. I felt completely exposed and humiliated, like my soul had been put on display. I went into the bathroom and stayed there for hours, looking at myself in the mirror and seeing my face distort into something ugly.<br><br>The next day the video was in a group chat with about 200 people from our dorm. It spread from there. People I didn't know were quoting the things I said to the wall. Someone made a meme. The girl I mentioned saw it. For weeks I couldn't walk across campus without someone saying one of my lines and laughing.<br><br>The trip itself was frightening, but the worst part was realising that people I thought were friends had done this.", 
"I'm an army medic. I'd seen a lot of injuries on deployment. Years later, I took mushrooms with my brother at a family cabin. At the peak, he cut his hand while chopping wood, quite a deep cut, a lot of blood. It wasn't life-threatening, but for me it was instantly the battlefield. I was back in a dusty compound with a soldier bleeding out under my hands, while I was actually wrapping my brother's hand in a kitchen towel. I did the right things, my hands knew what to do, but my mind was somewhere else entirely. I heard helicopters. I heard screaming. I saw my brother's face become the face of a young private I lost. When the bleeding was under control, I went outside and threw up and then lay down on the porch and shook for hours. My brother, with his bandaged hand, sat with me and kept saying 'I'm okay, I'm okay'. I couldn't believe him.", 
"Ich war bei einem Ayahuasca-Retreat in Portugal. In der zweiten Nacht ist ein anderer Teilnehmer, ein grosser Mann, ploetzlich aufgesprungen und hat angefangen zu schreien, dass wir alle Daemonen sind. Die Helfer haben versucht, ihn zu beruhigen, aber er hat sie weggestossen. Dann ist er auf mich losgegangen, weil ich ihm am naechsten lag. Er hat mich an den Schultern gepackt, geschuettelt und mir ins Gesicht geschrien. Ich war mitten in meinen eigenen Visionen und sah sein Gesicht als Fratze mit Hoernern. Ich dachte, ich werde jetzt getoetet. Zwei Helfer haben ihn schliesslich weggezogen und nach draussen gebracht. Ich lag den Rest der Nacht zitternd auf meiner Matte, unfaehig mich zu bewegen, und jedes Geraeusch von draussen hat mich zusammenzucken lassen. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass er zurueckkommt. Am naechsten Morgen war er weg, und die Leitung hat kaum darueber gesprochen.", 
"I'm a nervous flyer, and before a long-haul flight to visit family in Australia, a friend suggested I take a small dose of mushrooms to 'relax'. It was the worst advice I've ever received. I ate them in the airport toilet before boarding.<br><br>About an hour after take-off, the plane started to feel like a metal tube full of strangers breathing my air. The engine noise became a scream. Every bump of turbulence was the plane falling apart. I was certain we were going to crash and that everyone would die because of me, because I was carrying something evil onto the plane. I gripped the armrests until my hands cramped. The woman next to me asked if I was okay and I couldn't answer. Her face kept turning into a skull.<br><br>I went to the toilet and stayed there for a long time, until a flight attendant knocked and asked me to return to my seat because of turbulence. She noticed I was shaking and sweating and asked if I needed medical help. I said I was just a nervous flyer. She brought me water and checked on me every half hour, which was kind, but every time she came I thought she was about to say we were going down.<br><br>The effects faded after about five hours, but there were still nine hours to go. I spent them rigid in my seat, completely drained and terrified that it would come back. I didn't sleep. When we landed, I cried.", 
"I was at a party in a squat with ketamine and LSD going around. I'd taken both. Around 3am the police raided the building. There were maybe 20 officers in riot gear, with dogs. They came in shouting, with torches, and everyone panicked. I was in a k-hole on a mattress in a back room, barely able to move. Through the LSD, the officers looked like giant black insects with glowing eyes. One of them grabbed me by the arm and pulled me up, and I couldn't stand, so he dragged me. I was sure I was being taken to be executed. They made us all sit on the floor of the main hall with our hands on our heads. The dogs were barking right next to my face. Someone next to me was crying. I kept slipping in and out of the room in my head, sometimes I was there, sometimes I was floating in a dark void, and every time I came back, the dogs and the torches were still there. They searched us and took our names. I was released at dawn without charges. I walked home barefoot because someone had taken my shoes.", 
"Wir waren zu viert auf einem Segeltoern in Kroatien und hatten am dritten Tag beschlossen, in einer ruhigen Bucht LSD zu nehmen. Wir hatten nicht mit dem Wetter gerechnet. Am Nachmittag zog ein Sturm auf, und der Skipper, der als Einziger nuechtern war, entschied, dass wir die Bucht verlassen muessen, weil der Ankerplatz nicht sicher war.<br><br>Was dann kam, war der schlimmste Moment meines Lebens. Das Boot wurde von den Wellen hin und her geworfen, ich war seekrank und gleichzeitig auf dem Hoehepunkt des Trips. Das Meer sah aus wie ein riesiges Maul, das uns verschlingen will. Ich war mir sicher, dass wir kentern und ertrinken. Ich habe mich an die Reling geklammert und mich uebergeben und hatte das Gefuehl, dass ich jeden Moment ueber Bord gehe. Ich hoerte Stimmen im Wind, die mich riefen.<br><br>Der Skipper hat uns angeschrien, dass wir unter Deck gehen sollen, aber unten war es noch schlimmer, eng, dunkel, alles hat gewackelt und gerochen. Ich habe mich in eine Ecke gekauert und gebetet. Nach etwa zwei Stunden haben wir einen Hafen erreicht. Ich bin vom Boot gestolpert und habe mich auf den Steg gelegt und konnte nicht aufhoeren zu zittern. Die anderen waren auch fertig, aber ich glaube, mich hat es am schlimmsten erwischt.", 
"I'll try to tell this in order, because it's the only way I can make sense of it.<br><br>I'm a nurse, and three years ago I was at the end of a very bad year. My mother had died, my long relationship had ended, and work in the ICU during the last Covid wave had left me exhausted and numb. A colleague, also a nurse, told me about ayahuasca and how it had helped her process her grief. She gave me the contact of a group that met in a farmhouse a couple of hours from where I live. I signed up for a weekend with two ceremonies.<br><br>The first ceremony was hard but meaningful. I cried a lot about my mother, and at one point I felt her presence, warm and kind. I purged several times. I felt cleaner afterwards and I was glad I'd come.<br><br>The second night was different. The leader, a man in his sixties, said that the second night is when the medicine 'goes deeper', and he served a larger cup. About an hour after drinking, I started to see the ICU. Not as a memory, but as if I were there. The beeping of the monitors, the hiss of the ventilators, the smell of disinfectant. I saw the faces of patients I'd lost, one after another. There had been many. I'd never allowed myself to count them. In the vision they were lying in rows, and each one turned their head to look at me.<br><br>Then I saw my mother among them, in a hospital bed, on a ventilator. She had actually died at home, of cancer, not in an ICU. But in the vision she was there, and her eyes were open and terrified, and she was trying to say something and couldn't because of the tube.
