I was her nurse. I was supposed to help her. And I couldn't move. I stood there in my scrubs and watched the monitor flatline.<br><br>I started screaming. I was sure I was actually there. One of the helpers came and put his hand on my back and said something like 'you're safe, it's the medicine'. I couldn't hear it. His hand felt like a patient's hand, cold. I tore away from him and crawled across the floor to a corner.<br><br>After that, things fragmented. I lost any sense of being a person. I was the ICU. I was every alarm going off at once. I was the guilt of every death. I felt that I was being judged by all of the dead, and that the verdict was that I should join them. I remember thinking very clearly that the only way to make it stop was to die, and I started looking for a way out of the room. I think I tried to get to the door. Someone held me back. I fought them. I bit someone's arm, I found out later.<br><br>They had to hold me down, three of them. The leader came and sang over me and blew tobacco smoke in my face, which made me choke and feel like I was suffocating, like the patients who couldn't breathe. I could feel my lungs filling with fluid.<br><br>It lasted, I'm told, about four hours. When it finally began to ease, I was lying on a mattress in the corner, soaked in sweat and vomit, shaking. Someone had put a blanket over me. I didn't know who I was or where I was for a long time. The first thing I recognised was the smell of the woodstove, and I held on to it like a rope.<br><br>In the morning the leader told me that I had 'released a lot of collective trauma' and that I was a 'healer', and that this was my initiation. The person I had bitten had a bruise on his arm and was very kind about it. I couldn't look at anyone. I drove home, which I shouldn't have done, and I don't remember most of the drive.", 
```{r}
"Ich habe mit einem Freund 2C-B genommen. Nach einer Stunde hatte ich das Gefuehl, dass mein Gesicht nicht mehr mein Gesicht ist. Ich habe im Spiegel jemanden gesehen, den ich nicht kannte, und hatte panische Angst, dass ich so bleibe. Mein Freund hat mich beruhigt, und nach ein paar Stunden war es vorbei.", 
"Ich habe an einer Psilocybin-Studie fuer Menschen mit therapieresistenter Depression teilgenommen. Ich hatte grosse Hoffnungen. Die Sitzung fand in einem gemuetlich eingerichteten Raum in der Klinik statt, mit zwei Begleitern. Ich bekam eine hohe Dosis.<br><br>Nach etwa einer Stunde fuehlte ich mich, als wuerde ich in einen dunklen Schacht fallen. Alles, was ich an Hoffnung mitgebracht hatte, war weg. Ich sah mein Leben als eine endlose Kette von Versagen und Enttaeuschungen. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass meine Depression nicht eine Krankheit ist, sondern die Wahrheit ueber mich. Dass ich eben ein Mensch bin, der nicht gluecklich sein kann.<br><br>Dann kam das Gefuehl, eingesperrt zu sein. Der Raum wurde enger. Die Musik, die eigentlich beruhigend sein sollte, klang wie eine Totenmesse. Ich wollte die Augenmaske abnehmen und aufstehen, aber ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass ich mich nicht bewegen kann. Ich hoerte die Stimmen der Begleiter, aber sie klangen weit weg und gleichgueltig.<br><br>Die Begleiter haben mich nicht allein gelassen, das muss ich sagen. Eine von ihnen hat meine Hand gehalten und immer wieder gesagt, dass ich sicher bin. Aber ich konnte das nicht fuehlen. Das ging vielleicht drei Stunden so. Gegen Ende wurde es etwas leichter, und ich hatte einen kurzen Moment, in dem ich die Hand der Begleiterin wirklich gespuert habe, als etwas Warmes. Das war der einzige Lichtblick.", 
"My friends dared me to take mushrooms in the old cemetery at night. I thought it'd be a laugh. I started seeing figures standing between the graves, very still, watching. I was sure they were the dead and that they were angry we were there. I ran and fell over a gravestone and cut my knee. My friends thought it was funny until they saw how scared I was.", 
"I took LSD at home with my partner. We had done it before and it was usually a loving experience. This time, when we started to be intimate, I suddenly had a flood of memories of being assaulted at a party when I was 17. I had never told anyone, not even him, and I'd mostly pushed it out of my mind. But on LSD it was like it was happening right then. I could feel the weight on me, smell the alcohol. I pushed my partner away and screamed at him. He was shocked and confused. I hid under the duvet and shook for a long time. I couldn't explain. He thought he had done something wrong. Later in the night I told him what had happened when I was 17, and we both cried.", 
"Mushrooms. Nothing crazy happened, I just felt total dread for 5 hours for no reason.", 
"I drank ayahuasca at a small ceremony in Costa Rica. I purged a lot and then I saw my brother, who died of an overdose five years ago. He looked healthy and calm. He hugged me and I felt his love. It was overwhelming, I sobbed for hours. It was challenging because the grief I had been holding came up all at once, and for a while I couldn't breathe from crying.", 
"I'd been depressed for a long time and decided to try LSD on my own, hoping for something like a reset. I took two tabs in my flat. Within an hour, everything I disliked about myself was projected onto the walls like a slideshow. My ugliness, my failures, the time I'd been cruel to my little sister, the job I got fired from. A voice, which I recognised as my own but much harsher, commented on every image. You're pathetic. Nobody wants you. You should have never been born. I tried to turn on music, but every song had lyrics that seemed to agree with the voice.<br><br>I went into the bathroom and looked in the mirror, which was a terrible mistake. My face aged and rotted in front of me. Then it became my father's face, who left when I was five. I punched the mirror and cut my hand. There was blood in the sink, and on LSD the blood was the most vivid red I've ever seen, almost glowing. I sat on the bathroom floor and watched it drip and thought, very calmly, that it would be easier to let it all end.<br><br>I didn't. I don't know why. Maybe because a small part of me knew it was the drug. I wrapped my hand in a towel, crawled to my bed and lay there for ten hours under the covers, with the slideshow continuing on the inside of my eyelids. In the morning I went to A&E for stitches and told them I'd fallen.", 
"Took acid while visiting my grandmother in her care home, which was a stupid idea I'd had to 'see her soul'. The smells, the sounds of people moaning, my grandmother not recognising me, it all became a nightmare of decay and death. I fled to the car park and sat in the car for hours, crying.", 
"Wir waren im Urlaub in Portugal, meine Freundin und ich, und haben auf einer Klippe am Meer Pilze genommen. Zuerst war alles wunderschoen, das Meer glitzerte und ich fuehlte mich ihr sehr nahe. Dann hat sich etwas verschoben. Ich sah sie an und wusste ploetzlich nicht mehr, wer sie ist. Ihr Gesicht war mir voellig fremd. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass ich in einer Art Theaterstueck bin, in dem alle Rollen spielen und nur ich nicht weiss, worum es geht. Ich habe sie immer wieder gefragt, ob sie echt ist, und sie hat versucht, mich zu beruhigen, aber ihre Worte kamen bei mir nicht an. Dann fing die Zeit an, sich zu wiederholen. Ich habe dieselben Wellen, dieselben Moewen, dieselben Saetze immer und immer wieder erlebt. Ich hatte panische Angst, dass ich verrueckt geworden bin und dass das nie mehr aufhoert. Ich wollte nur noch weg von der Klippe, weil ich Angst hatte, dass ich springe, nicht weil ich sterben wollte, sondern um die Schleife zu durchbrechen. Meine Freundin hat mich am Arm genommen und zurueck zum Auto gefuehrt. Erst Stunden spaeter im Hotel hat die Schleife langsam aufgehoert.", 
"I was doing at-home ketamine treatment for depression through an online telehealth company. They send you lozenges and you do the session on your own, with a short video call before and after. During my fourth session I took the prescribed dose and lay down with my eyeshade. Something felt different. I left my body and couldn't find my way back. I had the feeling that I was dead and that my body was lying on the bed and no one would find it for days because I live alone. I couldn't move or speak. When it wore off I tried to call the provider's support line and got an automated message.", 
"I'm a trans woman. At the time of this experience, I had been living as myself for about three years and had started hormones two years before. I'd been struggling with anxiety and old family trauma, and I'd heard good things about ayahuasca from a friend. I found a retreat online that described itself as 'inclusive and heart-centred'. On the application form I wrote that I was trans. Nobody said anything about it.<br><br>When I arrived, the shaman, an older man from another country, seemed friendly. The facilitators were a European couple who translated for him. On the first evening there was a group circle where we introduced ourselves. When it was my turn, I said my name and that I'm a trans woman. The shaman said something to the facilitators, and they hesitated before translating. Eventually the woman said that the shaman 'honoured my journey' and that the medicine would 'help me find balance in my energies'. I felt a little uneasy but let it go.<br><br>The first ceremony was fine, mostly physical, a lot of purging. In the second ceremony, the shaman came to sit in front of me to do a 'healing'. He blew tobacco smoke over me and sang. Then he started speaking, and the male facilitator translated in a low voice. He said that he saw a 'masculine spirit trapped and suffering' inside me, and that he would help free it. He said the 'confusion' I was in was caused by a dark energy that had entered me in childhood. He pressed his hand hard on my chest, where my breasts are, and said he was 'removing the false feminine'.<br><br>I was deep in the medicine. I couldn't speak. I couldn't move. I wanted to scream at him to stop, but it was like my body belonged to someone else. And worse, part of me, in that state, started to believe him. I saw images of myself as a boy, the boy I was forced to be for so long, crying in a dark room. I saw my father's face, telling me to 'man up'. I felt that everything I had built, my name, my body, my life, was a lie and that I was being punished for it. I felt my identity crumbling, and I didn't know who I was anymore. Not a woman, not a man, just a shattered thing on the floor.<br><br>He went on singing for what felt like hours. At one point he called me by my old name, the name I haven't used in years, which I had never told anyone at the retreat. I still don't know how he knew it, maybe it was in my passport, which they had copied for registration. Hearing it in that state was like being thrown back into my childhood bedroom.<br><br>When the ceremony ended, I crawled to my bed and lay there shaking until morning. At breakfast the female facilitator came to me and said that she understood it was a 'challenging' night, but that the shaman was 'very powerful' and saw things we couldn't. She said that some people come to the medicine with 'mental constructs' that need to be released. I told her I wanted to leave. She said that leaving in the middle of the process could be dangerous for my spirit. I left anyway, that afternoon, with a taxi to the nearest town and a bus to the airport.<br><br>On the bus I kept touching my chest where his hand had been and feeling sick.", 
"I was at a warehouse rave, on LSD and a bit of MDMA. My friend Sam was also taking GHB, which I didn't know. Around 3am I found him slumped in a corner, not responding. His lips were blue and his breathing was very slow and weird. I was tripping hard and I couldn't tell if it was real or a hallucination. I shook him and he didn't wake up. I screamed for help and a couple of people came over and one of them knew first aid and said he wasn't breathing properly.<br><br>Someone called an ambulance. The first aider started rescue breathing and told me to keep talking to Sam. I held his hand and talked to him and I was convinced he was dead and that his soul was floating out of his body. I could see it, like a grey mist rising. The music was still pounding and the strobe was going and I was in hell.<br><br>The paramedics took him away. I wasn't allowed in the ambulance. I sat outside on the pavement until dawn, not knowing if he was alive. My phone died. I walked home, which took two hours, seeing his blue face in every shop window.<br><br>Sam survived. He was in intensive care for two days. When I finally visited him he was fine and joked about it.", 
"Bad trip on mushrooms, I thought I was going insane and would never come back to normal.", 
"I used to be a very rational person who saw psychedelics as just a chemical curiosity. I took a large dose of mushrooms with friends at a holiday rental. At some point I closed my eyes and found myself in front of an enormous being, made of light and eyes and wings, the kind of thing you see in medieval paintings of angels. It was so huge and so overwhelming that I felt crushed by its presence. It looked at me and I felt it knew everything about me, every thought I'd ever had, and it was not pleased. It said, without words, 'you have wasted your life'. I fell to my knees, physically, in the room. My friends said I was on the floor for an hour, crying and apologising to nobody. I felt as if my whole worldview had been smashed. I didn't know what was real anymore. I had no framework for what happened. It was beyond terrifying.", 
"LSD and then a few balloons of laughing gas. I stood up too fast, fainted and hit my head on a table. Woke up not knowing who or where I was, blood on my face. Scary for an hour.", 
"Ich habe bei einer Zeremonie in Spanien San Pedro getrunken. Nach etwa zwei Stunden wurde mir extrem uebel, und ich hatte das Gefuehl, vergiftet worden zu sein. Mein Koerper fuehlte sich schwer und fremd an, mein Herz raste. Die Leiterin sagte, das sei normal, aber ich war mir sicher, dass ich sterbe. Ich lag stundenlang in der Sonne, unfaehig mich zu bewegen, und hatte Todesangst. Spaeter habe ich mich uebergeben, aber die Panik ging nicht weg.", 
"I'll describe this as carefully as I can, because for a long time I couldn't describe it at all.<br><br>I was 34, a primary school teacher, married, no children yet. My husband and I had been trying for a baby for two years without success and it was putting a lot of strain on us. A close friend of mine had done a psilocybin retreat in the Netherlands and came back glowing, saying it had helped her let go of years of grief. I booked the same retreat, partly hoping it would help me with the stress of trying to conceive, and partly, I think, because I wanted to feel something other than disappointment for a weekend.<br><br>The retreat was in a renovated farmhouse. There were ten participants and three facilitators, all very warm. On the first evening we sat in a circle and shared our intentions. I said I wanted to make peace with not being in control of my body. Everyone nodded. The facilitators talked about 'surrender' and 'trusting the medicine'.<br><br>The ceremony began the next morning. We drank truffle tea, lay down on mats with eyeshades, and the music began. The dose was high. I remember the come-up as a kind of heavy, sweet sinking, as if the floor were turning into honey. For about an hour it was beautiful. I saw fields of flowers, I felt my body as warm and alive, I cried softly about the babies I hadn't had.<br><br>Then the flowers turned into something else. They became wombs, hundreds of them, opening and closing, and every one was empty. I heard a sound like a heartbeat, but it was slowing, slowing, until it stopped. I understood, with absolute certainty, that I would never have a child. That my body was a barren place, that I had been born broken. The certainty was total. It wasn't a thought, it was a knowledge that went through every cell.<br><br>Then something worse happened. I started to see children, not my children, but children I knew: the children in my class. I saw their faces, one after another, and each one turned grey and still. I felt that I was being shown that I was a danger to children, that something in me was poisonous, that this was why my body wouldn't let me have one. I know how irrational this sounds now, but in that state it was the most real truth I'd ever encountered.<br><br>I tore off my eyeshade. The room was full of people lying on mats, and the facilitators moving quietly between them, and it looked like a field hospital, or a morgue. A facilitator came over and asked what was happening. I couldn't explain. I said 'I'm poison, I'm poison' over and over. She put her hand on my belly, I think meaning to comfort me, and I screamed, because that was exactly the place where the poison was.<br><br>I tried to get up and leave, but my legs wouldn't hold me, and I fell against the wall. Two facilitators guided me to a smaller side room with a mattress and stayed with me. One of them held my hand. I was sobbing so hard that I couldn't breathe properly, and I started to hyperventilate, and my hands cramped into claws. I thought I was dying. Part of me wanted to.<br><br>I went somewhere after that. I don't know how long it lasted. There was no room, no facilitators, no me. Just an endless grey plain with a cold wind, and the knowledge that I was alone and would always be alone, and that nothing would ever grow there. I wandered on that plain for what felt like years.<br><br>When I came back, it was afternoon. The facilitators were still there. One of them was crying too. They had been with me for five hours. They gave me water and a blanket and sat with me until the evening. In the closing circle I couldn't speak. My friend's glowing description of the retreat kept going through my head like a cruel joke.<br><br>I went home the next day. I told my husband it had been 'intense'. I didn't tell him the rest for months.", 
"I want to write this out fully, because the short version, 'I had a bad trip and ended up in a psychiatric hospital', doesn't capture what it was like, and because I think the details of how it went wrong could help someone.<br><br>Background: I was 24, working in a call centre, living with two flatmates. I'd had depression in my teens, but I'd been okay for a couple of years. I'd taken mushrooms twice and LSD once, all small doses, all positive. My flatmate K had just come back from a festival with some LSD tabs and said they were 'quite strong, maybe split one'. I didn't split it. I took the whole tab on a Saturday afternoon. K took half, and our other flatmate didn't take anything but was home.<br><br>The first two hours: the come-up was faster and stronger than anything I'd felt before. Within forty minutes the carpet was rippling and the walls were covered in patterns. That part was fun. We put on music and lay on the floor. K was laughing a lot. I remember feeling very happy and close to her.<br><br>The turn: around the two-hour mark, I went to the bathroom. I looked in the mirror and my pupils were enormous, black holes. I stared into them and felt like I was falling in. Behind my eyes there was a corridor, and at the end of the corridor something was waiting. I knew I shouldn't look, but I couldn't stop. When I finally pulled away from the mirror, I felt that something had followed me out. A presence behind my left shoulder. I turned around and nothing was there, but the feeling stayed.<br><br>I went back to the living room and tried to tell K. She said 'it's just the acid' and turned the music up. The music had changed. It was something with a heavy bass, and every beat felt like a footstep coming closer. The presence was still behind me. I started glancing over my shoulder every few seconds. K thought it was funny at first, then she stopped laughing.<br><br>The fragmentation: the next part is hard to describe in order, because it wasn't in order. I remember the living room lights getting brighter and brighter until everything was white. I remember being in the kitchen with a glass of water and not knowing what water was for. I remember sitting on the floor of my bedroom, holding my knees, rocking. I remember hearing a voice, very clearly, saying my name and then 'it's over now'. I took that to mean my life was over. I remember lying on my bed and feeling my body sinking into it, through it, into the floor, into the building, into the earth, until there was no body and no me, just a heavy, dark pressure and a voice repeating 'it's over now'.<br><br>The flatmates: our sober flatmate, J, came into my room at some point. He told me later that I was lying on the bed with my eyes open, not responding, and that when he touched my arm I screamed and backed into the corner. He said I kept saying 'it's over, it's over, I'm already dead'. He tried to talk to me for half an hour. I didn't recognise him. I thought he was the thing from behind the mirror, wearing J's face. K was in her own room, crying, too scared to come in.<br><br>The ambulance: J called an ambulance after about an hour of trying to calm me down, because I had started hitting my head against the wall. Two paramedics came, a man and a woman. The woman was very calm and kind. She crouched down and talked to me in a quiet voice. I remember her saying 'you've taken something, it's making you feel this way, it will wear off'. For a moment that made sense, like a door opening. Then the door closed again and I was sure she was lying, that this was how they took you to the place where the dead go.<br><br>The hospital: in A&E they gave me a sedative. I remember the needle and a very cold feeling spreading up my arm. I slept, or something like sleep. When I woke up it was night and I was on a trolley in a corridor, and I didn't know how much time had passed. The LSD was still working, but more weakly, and the sedative had made everything heavy and muddy. A doctor came and asked me questions. I couldn't answer most of them. I told her I thought I had died. She wrote something down.<br><br>Because I couldn't say clearly that I wasn't going to hurt myself, and because of the head-banging, they admitted me to the psychiatric ward for observation. I was there for four days. The first two days I was still not right. The presence behind my shoulder was still there. Every door slamming made me jump. The other patients scared me, though they were mostly just as frightened as I was. I didn't sleep much. I was ashamed and terrified that I'd broken my mind forever.<br><br>On the third day I started to feel more like myself. A psychiatrist talked to me for a long time and said it was very likely a drug-induced episode and that it should pass. On the fourth day they let me go home. My mother came to pick me up. She didn't say a word in the car. I could feel her disappointment and fear like heat.<br><br>Afterwards I found out that the tabs K had brought were tested by someone else at the festival and were around 250ug each, maybe more. I had taken a dose far higher than I'd ever had, with no preparation, in a setting that wasn't really safe, after years of depression I'd thought was behind me.", 
"I was a second year student and took LSD with my roommate in our dorm. We had done it once before and it was fun. This time, maybe two hours in, I was looking out the window at the night sky and I suddenly understood that the universe is going to end. Not in a scientific way, but I felt it, the heat death, all the stars going out one by one, and nothing left, forever. And that everything I do, everyone I love, all of it is just a tiny flicker before the endless dark. My roommate was laughing at something on his laptop and it seemed obscene to me that he could laugh. I sat on the floor with my back against the bed and couldn't stop thinking about infinity. It felt like my mind was being stretched beyond what it could hold. I asked him if he ever thought about how nothing matters, and he said 'dude you're just tripping' and put on some music. I spent the rest of the night staring at the wall feeling an indescribable dread.", 
"DMT. I lived through my mother's death in vivid detail, at her bedside, holding her cold hand. She's alive and well. It felt completely real. I came back sobbing and couldn't stop for an hour.", 
"Ich war auf einem Microdosing-Retreat, bei dem auch intensive Atemarbeit gemacht wurde. Waehrend der Atemuebung bekam ich eine heftige Panikattacke, habe hyperventiliert, meine Haende haben sich verkrampft und ich konnte sie nicht mehr bewegen. Die Leiterin hat gesagt, ich solle einfach weiteratmen. Ich hatte Todesangst.", 
"I had a very bad experience with ayahuasca that I didn't recognise as a bad experience until much later. I was at a retreat where the facilitators framed everything as healing: if you screamed, you were releasing trauma; if you shook, you were letting go of stuck energy; if you felt terror, the medicine was showing you your shadow. During my third ceremony I had the strongest experience of my life. I was being torn apart by animals, again and again, a jaguar, a pack of dogs, giant birds. Each time I felt the pain and the fear of dying. Between the attacks I was rebuilt, only to be torn apart again. It went on for hours. I screamed and begged. The facilitators sang louder and told me to surrender. Afterwards they said I had been through a 'shamanic dismemberment', which is apparently a well-known initiatory experience, and that I should feel honoured. I believed them, so I didn't ask for help when things went wrong afterwards.", 
"I smoked DMT at home, and my partner, who was supposed to sit for me, left the room halfway through to take a phone call. I came back to an empty room and felt totally abandoned and lost. I didn't know where I was or if I was alive. I lay there alone for maybe half an hour after the main effects wore off, crying and calling for him. When he came back he didn't understand why I was so upset.", 
"Ich habe zusammen mit meiner Schwester Pilze genommen, an einem Sommertag im Garten unserer Eltern, waehrend sie im Urlaub waren. Meine Schwester hat irgendwann angefangen zu erzaehlen, dass sie als Kind von unserem Onkel missbraucht wurde. Das wusste ich nicht. Sie hat geweint, und ich war mitten im Trip und konnte nicht klar denken. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass der Garten sich in das Haus unseres Onkels verwandelt und dass ich alles mitansehen muss. Ich habe Bilder gesehen, die ich nicht sehen wollte, und war unfaehig, meiner Schwester richtig beizustehen. Ich habe sie nur festgehalten und mit ihr geweint. Gleichzeitig hatte ich das Gefuehl, dass ich versagt habe, weil ich als grosser Bruder nie etwas gemerkt habe. Der Rest des Nachmittags war ein einziger Albtraum. Wir sassen bis zum Abend unter dem Apfelbaum und haben kaum gesprochen.", 
"Took 2C-E at a friend's place. The body load was awful. My heart was pounding and I felt like my veins were full of electricity, I couldn't sit still. I thought I was overdosing. Lasted for hours and I couldn't relax at all. My friend kept saying it would pass but it felt endless.", 
"I was part of a spiritual community for about two years, led by a man who called himself a teacher and who ran regular ayahuasca ceremonies. I joined at a vulnerable time, after my divorce, and at first it felt like finding a family. Over time it became more controlling. We were encouraged to give money, to spend all our weekends there, to distance ourselves from 'low-vibration' people, which slowly came to include most of our families and old friends.<br><br>The ceremony I'm describing was the one that broke me. The teacher had asked me, in private, to give up contact with my mother, who had been worried about me and had criticised the group. I'd refused. That night, in the ceremony, after the brew had taken hold, he sat in front of me and started a long 'transmission'. He said that my mother was a vessel of dark energy, that she had been sabotaging my soul since my birth, that my depression, my divorce, all my suffering came from her. He said the medicine was showing me this truth and that if I didn't cut her off, I would be lost.<br><br>In that state I saw what he said. I saw my mother's face turning black and twisted. I saw a cord connecting us, made of something rotten. I saw scenes from my childhood reinterpreted, every time she'd been strict, every time she'd been sad, as evidence. I felt enormous fear and grief. Part of me was screaming that this was wrong, that my mother loves me. But the louder voice was his, and the medicine seemed to amplify it.<br><br>He made me 'cut the cord' symbolically with a feather, in front of the group. Everyone was singing. I was sobbing and shaking. I felt my sense of who I was dissolving, as if I had no past, no family, nothing except the group and him.<br><br>Afterwards, the others hugged me and congratulated me on my 'liberation'. I went home the next morning and blocked my mother's number. I didn't speak to her for eight months.", 
"Ich habe an einem Psilocybin-Retreat in den Niederlanden teilgenommen. Ich hatte vorher eine Absicht formuliert: Ich wollte meine Beziehung zu meiner Mutter verstehen. Schon nach kurzer Zeit kamen Bilder aus meiner Kindheit. Ich sah mich als kleines Maedchen, allein in meinem Zimmer, waehrend meine Mutter im Nebenzimmer trank und schrie. Ich spuerte die ganze Angst und Einsamkeit von damals in meinem Koerper. Ich habe am ganzen Koerper gezittert und laut geweint. Die Begleiterin war offensichtlich ueberfordert, sie hat mir nur gesagt, ich solle atmen, und ist dann zu anderen Teilnehmern gegangen. Ich lag da und hatte das Gefuehl, wieder ganz allein zu sein, genau wie damals. Das hat es noch schlimmer gemacht. Gegen Ende der Erfahrung wurde es ruhiger, und ich hatte einen kurzen Moment von Mitgefuehl mit dem kleinen Maedchen. Aber die meiste Zeit war es einfach nur schmerzhaft.", 
"I had a very strong experience on mushrooms in my early twenties that I still think about. I took them with my then-girlfriend in her parents' garden while they were on holiday. About an hour in, I lay on the lawn and looked up at the sky, and the sky opened. I mean it literally looked like it was splitting apart, and behind it was a huge, unimaginably old darkness. I felt that something was looking at me from that darkness, and that it had always been looking at me, my whole life, and that it was neither good nor evil, just completely indifferent. Under that gaze I felt myself shrink to nothing. My memories, my plans, my love for my girlfriend, all of it became tiny and pointless, like dust.<br><br>I tried to get up and go inside, but the house seemed impossibly far away, and the garden kept stretching. My girlfriend was sitting next to me and I couldn't make her understand. She kept saying 'look at the flowers', and the flowers were beautiful, but I knew they were a thin coating over the darkness. I started crying and couldn't stop. I clung to the grass because I felt that if I let go, I would fall upwards into the sky and disappear.<br><br>It lasted for maybe three or four hours. In the evening it faded, and we went inside and watched a cartoon, which was the only thing I could handle. The colours of the cartoon were comforting, like a children's room after a nightmare. But that night, when I lay in bed and closed my eyes, I could still feel the darkness behind the ceiling.", 
"Ich habe in einer Phase grosser Lebenskrise allein LSD genommen, weil ich gehofft hatte, Antworten zu finden. Stattdessen bin ich in eine Gedankenschleife geraten, in der ich immer wieder dieselben Fragen gestellt habe: Wer bin ich? Was ist echt? Warum lebe ich? Jede Antwort hat sofort zu einer neuen Frage gefuehrt, und irgendwann hat sich alles aufgeloest, auch das Ich, das die Fragen stellt. Ich lag auf dem Boden und hatte das Gefuehl, dass es mich nicht gibt und nie gegeben hat. Das hat sich angefuehlt wie Sterben, nur ohne Ende. Ich habe stundenlang auf die Decke gestarrt, unfaehig, mich zu bewegen. Erst als es dunkel wurde und ich Hunger bekam, kam ich langsam wieder zu mir. Ich habe mir ein Brot geschmiert und dabei geweint, weil es so etwas Normales war.", 
"Ich war mit einer Freundin auf Reisen in Thailand und wir sind zu einer Full-Moon-Party gegangen. Dort hat uns jemand Pilz-Shakes verkauft, und ich habe einen ganzen getrunken, ohne zu wissen, wie stark er ist. Nach einer Stunde war ich voellig weg. Die Musik, die Feuer-Shows, die tausend Menschen am Strand, alles hat sich zu einem Albtraum vermischt. Ich habe meine Freundin verloren und bin am Strand umhergeirrt. Irgendwann habe ich bemerkt, dass meine Tasche weg war, mit Pass, Geld und Handy. Ich hatte panische Angst, nie wieder nach Hause zu kommen. Dann kamen zwei Maenner in Uniform, ich weiss nicht, ob es echte Polizisten waren, und haben mich gefragt, ob ich Drogen genommen habe. Sie haben gedroht, mich ins Gefaengnis zu bringen, wenn ich nicht bezahle. Ich hatte kein Geld. Sie haben mich eine Weile festgehalten und angeschrien, bis sie mich irgendwann gehen liessen. Ich habe bis zum Morgen hinter einem Boot gesessen und gezittert. Meine Freundin hat mich am naechsten Tag gefunden.", 
"Ich war mit Freunden in einem Club in Berlin und hatte LSD genommen. Ich bin irgendwann allein durch den Club gelaufen und in einen Bereich geraten, wo viele Leute halbnackt waren und Sex hatten. Ich war voellig ueberfordert, alles war laut, dunkel und eng, und ich fand den Ausgang nicht. Fremde Menschen haben mich angefasst. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, in der Hoelle zu sein, und konnte nicht atmen. Irgendwann hat mich ein Tuersteher rausgefuehrt.", 
"I was at a large psytrance festival. On the third day, already sleep-deprived, I took a strong dose of LSD and then later someone gave me some 'extra' which I think was DMT or something similar. I lost all sense of the festival. I was in a different world, made of fractal geometry, endless and shifting, and I had no body. I felt that my consciousness was being stretched across infinity, thinner and thinner. Then the geometry started to break apart, like glass shattering, and behind it was black nothing. I felt myself being sucked in. I fought it with everything I had, but there was nothing to fight with.<br><br>When I came back, I was lying in a field far from the main stages, in the dark, alone. I had no idea how I'd got there. My phone and wallet were gone. I was wearing one shoe. I didn't know which day it was, or what country I was in. The music from the stages, far away, sounded like a huge machine grinding. I wandered for hours in the dark trying to find my tent. Every person I saw looked like a hollow shell. I asked a few people where I was, and they laughed. Someone gave me water. Eventually a festival volunteer found me and brought me to the welfare tent, where they kept me until morning and eventually found my friends through a lost-and-found board.<br><br>I'd lost about 14 hours that I can't account for.", 
"Nach einer schmerzhaften Trennung wollte ich mit Pilzen allein im Wald eine Art Heilungsreise machen. Ich hatte meinen Hund dabei, einen jungen Mischling, den ich nach der Trennung behalten hatte. Er war fuer mich das Wichtigste in dieser Zeit. Ich nahm etwa 3 Gramm und setzte mich mit ihm auf eine Lichtung.<br><br>Am Anfang war es schoen. Die Baeume leuchteten, ich habe viel geweint und mich mit dem Hund verbunden gefuehlt. Dann, auf dem Hoehepunkt, ist er ploetzlich einem Reh hinterhergerannt. Ich habe ihn gerufen, aber er kam nicht zurueck. Ich wollte ihm nachlaufen, aber ich konnte kaum stehen, der Waldboden bewegte sich unter meinen Fuessen wie Wasser. Ich bin hingefallen und habe gerufen und geschrien, immer wieder seinen Namen.<br><br>Ich habe mich auf die Suche gemacht und bin durch den Wald gestolpert. Es wurde langsam dunkel. Jeder Schatten war fuer mich ein Hund, und dann wieder nicht. Ich hoerte ihn bellen, aus allen Richtungen gleichzeitig. Ich war mir sicher, dass er tot ist und dass es meine Schuld ist, weil ich ihn nicht an die Leine genommen habe. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, alles zu verlieren, was ich liebe, zuerst meine Beziehung und jetzt ihn.<br><br>Irgendwann kam ich an eine Landstrasse. Und da lag er. Ein Auto hatte ihn angefahren, und der Fahrer war weitergefahren. Er lebte noch, aber er war schwer verletzt. Ich weiss nicht, wie ich es geschafft habe, aber ich habe ihn auf den Arm genommen und bin die Strasse entlanggelaufen, bis ein Auto angehalten hat. Die Frau hat uns zu einem Tiernotdienst gefahren. Auf der Fahrt habe ich die ganze Zeit sein Blut an meinen Haenden gesehen, und die Farben sind explodiert, und ich dachte, ich verliere den Verstand.<br><br>Er ist in der Nacht gestorben. Ich war noch nicht ganz nuechtern, als mir die Tieraerztin das gesagt hat. Ich habe sie angeschrien und dann nur noch geweint. Die Frau, die uns gefahren hat, hat mich nach Hause gebracht. Ich weiss bis heute nicht ihren Namen.", 
"I thought it would be a beautiful idea to take a small dose of LSD and visit an art museum. I'd read about people doing it. The first rooms were wonderful, the colours in the paintings glowed and moved. Then I came into a room with old religious paintings: martyrs, saints being tortured, the Last Judgement. The figures started to move. The saints turned their heads and looked at me. The demons in the Last Judgement crawled out of the frame. I could hear the screams of the damned.<br><br>I sat down on a bench in the middle of the room and couldn't get up. I felt that I was in the painting, being judged, and that I'd be sent down with the damned. A security guard came over and asked if I was okay, and his uniform and stern face made him look like one of the angels with swords. I said I was fine, but I was shaking. He asked if I needed a doctor, and I panicked and ran out of the museum. Outside, the statues on the facade were watching me. I sat in a park for hours under a tree, curled up, waiting for the judgement to end.", 
"Ich habe in einem Retreat Ayahuasca getrunken und eine sehr schwere Nacht erlebt. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass sich Schlangen um meinen Hals winden und mich erwuergen. Ich habe keine Luft mehr bekommen und gedacht, dass ich sterbe. Die Leiterin hat gesagt, das sei eine Reinigung meines Halschakras. Fuer mich war es einfach nur Todesangst, die Stunden gedauert hat.", 
"Pilze bei Freunden. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass mein Gesicht schmilzt, und konnte keinen Spiegel mehr ansehen. Ich dachte, dass ich so bleibe und dass jeder sehen kann, wie haesslich ich in Wirklichkeit bin.", 
"I was taking an SSRI for depression and hadn't told the retreat about it, because I was afraid they wouldn't let me participate. I'd stopped it two days before, thinking that would be enough. It wasn't. About an hour after drinking ayahuasca, I started sweating heavily, my muscles were twitching, my jaw was clenching, and my temperature went up. My heart was pounding. I became extremely agitated and confused. The visions were chaotic and frightening, like being inside a malfunctioning machine. I knew something was wrong with my body. The facilitator realised it might be serotonin syndrome and they drove me to a hospital, where I was treated with cooling and medication. I was in intensive care overnight. I could have died.", 
"Ich hatte eine sehr schwierige Erfahrung mit LSD, bei der ich das Gefuehl hatte, mich komplett aufzuloesen. Ich wusste nicht mehr, wer ich bin, und hatte das Gefuehl, dass es mich nie gegeben hat. Das war schlimmer als jede Angst, die ich kannte.", 
"Ich war auf einer Technoparty und habe LSD genommen. Spaeter hat mir jemand noch Ketamin angeboten, und ich habe ohne nachzudenken eine Line gezogen. Das war ein riesiger Fehler. Ploetzlich war mein Koerper weg, ich konnte meine Arme und Beine nicht mehr spueren, und die Musik wurde zu einem einzigen Droehnen. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, in eine Art Tunnel gezogen zu werden, und dass ich da nicht mehr rauskomme. Die Zeit hat sich wiederholt, immer und immer wieder dieselbe Sekunde. Ich habe versucht, meinen Freunden etwas zu sagen, aber ich wusste nicht mehr, wie Sprechen geht. Irgendwann sass ich draussen an der Wand, eine Freundin hat meine Hand gehalten. Ich wusste nicht, ob sie echt ist. Das ging so etwa zwei Stunden, danach kam ich langsam zurueck, aber die Welt sah noch lange seltsam flach und kuenstlich aus.", 
"I took a high dose of mushrooms, about 5 grams, at home with my partner. It was my idea, I'd read about 'heroic doses'. She took a smaller dose to look after me.<br><br>About an hour and a half in, I looked at her and something was wrong. She looked exactly like her, but I knew with absolute certainty that it wasn't her. It was someone, or something, wearing her face. Her movements were slightly off, her voice was slightly wrong, like a recording. I tried to stay calm and test her. I asked her questions only she would know. She answered them correctly, which made it worse, because it meant the impostor had access to her memories. I started thinking that the real her was somewhere else, maybe dead, and this thing had taken her place.<br><br>I locked myself in the bedroom with our cat. The cat was the only thing I trusted. I sat in the corner holding him and listening to her knocking on the door and calling my name, and every time I heard her voice I felt sick with fear. I was also sure the thing could change shape and might come through the walls. I could see the walls bulging.<br><br>She called my brother, who came over. I didn't trust him either. They talked to me through the door for hours. Eventually I fell asleep, or passed out, holding the cat.<br><br>The next morning I woke up and the drug had worn off, but the feeling hadn't fully gone. I looked at her and I knew in my head it was her, but there was a tiny voice saying 'are you sure?'. That voice lasted for days. I couldn't kiss her. I'd test her with questions. She was very hurt and scared. My brother took me to a doctor on the third day.", 
"I took mushrooms at a friend's place with four other people. We'd planned it well, with music and snacks and a sober friend. For me, around the peak, the room filled with a feeling of judgement. Everyone looked at me as if they knew some terrible secret about me. I became sure that I had done something unforgivable, though I couldn't remember what, and that they had all gathered to confront me. Every word they said had a double meaning. When someone offered me orange juice, I thought it was poisoned as punishment. I went into the bathroom and locked the door and sat in the bathtub. The sober friend talked to me through the door for two hours, telling me they loved me. I didn't believe a single word.", 
"Ich war mit meinem Freund auf Pilzen in seiner Wohnung, als ploetzlich seine Ex-Freundin vor der Tuer stand und Sturm geklingelt hat. Sie war betrunken und hat geschrien, dass sie sich etwas antut, wenn er nicht aufmacht. Er hat aufgemacht, und es gab einen furchtbaren Streit mit viel Geschrei und Weinen. Ich sass im Schlafzimmer und habe alles mitgehoert, und durch die Pilze war es, als wuerde der Streit direkt in meinem Kopf stattfinden. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass sie gleich ins Zimmer kommt und mich angreift. Irgendwann hat er die Polizei gerufen, weil sie nicht gehen wollte. Ich habe die ganze Zeit im Schlafzimmer gesessen und mich nicht bewegt.", 
"Ego death on 5 grams. Thought I would never come back to being a person.", 
"Ich war mit drei Freunden in einem Ferienhaus, wir hatten Pilztee getrunken. Am Anfang war alles lustig, dann fing ich an, die Gespraeche der anderen merkwuerdig zu finden. Ich hatte das Gefuehl, dass sie ueber mich reden und sich ueber mich lustig machen. Jeder Blick, jedes Lachen schien gegen mich gerichtet zu sein. Ich wurde immer misstrauischer und war mir irgendwann sicher, dass sie mir etwas ins Getraenk getan hatten und mich loswerden wollten. Ich bin aus dem Haus gerannt, barfuss, mitten in der Nacht, und in den Wald gelaufen. Ich habe mich hinter einem Baum versteckt und gezittert, ich hoerte Stimmen, die meinen Namen gerufen haben, und dachte, sie suchen mich, um mir etwas anzutun. Es war kalt und dunkel, ich hatte ueberall Kratzer an den Fuessen. Irgendwann kam ein Auto, und es war die Polizei, weil meine Freunde sie gerufen hatten. Ich habe mich gewehrt, weil ich dachte, die Polizisten gehoeren auch dazu. Sie haben mich ins Krankenhaus gebracht, wo ich die Nacht verbracht habe. Am naechsten Tag habe ich mich unglaublich geschaemt. Die Freundschaft zu zweien von den dreien ist danach zerbrochen, weil ich mich nicht mehr in ihre Naehe getraut habe."
), text_postacute = c("In the months after, I had panic attacks that always involved breathing. I'd suddenly feel like I couldn't get air and I'd gasp. It would happen in the shower, when I put my face in water, when I had a cold and my nose was blocked, and sometimes for no reason at all, lying in bed. I avoided swimming completely, which I used to love. I had nightmares about water. I also had some days of feeling very far away from myself.<br><br>At the same time, I learned something big about my life. Discovering the near-drowning explained a lot about my lifelong anxiety, my fear of losing control, my need to always know where the exits are. In a strange way, it was a relief to finally have a reason.", 
"For months I had a problem with 'reality checking'. I'd wake up in the morning and not be sure if I was really awake. I'd pinch myself, check clocks, look at text. If something seemed slightly off, I'd panic that I was back in the loop. I had derealisation and a lot of anxiety. Dreams became frightening because I couldn't always tell them apart from waking life. It slowly faded over about a year.", 
"For months I had nightmares about being lost in the forest and about my father's face. I couldn't go into woods or even parks with lots of trees without my heart racing. I'd always loved hiking and that was taken away. I also fell into a depression, which I think was the grief for my dad that I hadn't processed, made worse by the shame of what I'd done. I felt like a complete idiot and a burden on my family.<br>Looking back after two years, I've come to see the experience as the moment when my grief finally broke through. I hadn't cried at his funeral. The trip forced me to feel it, even if in the most dangerous possible way.", 
"For several months I had a sense that I might really be in hell and that normal life was the illusion. It made me depressed and anxious. I'd stare at the flames on the stove and feel a jolt of panic. I also became very preoccupied with religion and sin, which I never was before, and spent hours reading about the afterlife at night.", 
"Seitdem hasse ich Silvester. Ich verbringe den Jahreswechsel in einem abgelegenen Ferienhaus, weit weg vom Feuerwerk. Laute Knalle lassen mich das ganze Jahr ueber zusammenzucken.", 
"Seitdem sehe ich staendig Nachbilder und ein leichtes Flimmern, vor allem bei wenig Licht. Am Anfang hatte ich deswegen grosse Angst und dachte, mein Gehirn ist kaputt. Ich hatte auch einige Monate lang Derealisation und konnte mich schlecht konzentrieren. Die Angst ist inzwischen weniger, aber die visuellen Stoerungen sind nach drei Jahren immer noch da. Manchmal frage ich mich, ob ich jemals wieder 'normal' sehen werde.", 
"Nach dieser Nacht hatte ich grosse Angst vor Krankenhaeusern und Polizei. Ich habe mich vor meiner Mitbewohnerin geschaemt und bin ein paar Wochen spaeter ausgezogen. Ich hatte noch lange das Bild des kahlen Zimmers mit der Tuer ohne Klinke im Kopf, vor allem nachts. Ich fuehlte mich bestraft dafuer, dass es mir schlecht ging, und habe mich danach erst recht nicht getraut, mit jemandem ueber meine duesteren Gedanken zu sprechen.", 
"I felt shaky and anxious for a few weeks and stayed away from the subway. But mostly I came out of it with a strange gratitude for strangers, and for that man in particular.", 
"I fell into a deep depression. The trip made me believe the voice that says I'm worthless, and it took a long time for that belief to loosen. I had flashbacks to the school toilets, more vivid than before the trip. I couldn't use public toilets for months, and the smell of bleach would make me shake. I started hitting myself again occasionally when I was upset, which I hadn't done in years. I felt betrayed by the influencer and stupid for believing him. I also became very isolated because I felt ashamed of what happened.", 
"For a long time after the retreat I couldn't be in the dark. I slept with all the lights on, and I bought a small light for the bathroom so I'd never have to be in darkness, even for a second. Power cuts were terrifying. When I closed my eyes I sometimes saw the eyes on the walls opening.<br><br>I had the persistent sense of a presence near me, especially at night. I'd feel something sitting on the edge of the bed. I knew it wasn't real but I felt it. This went on for about eight months.<br><br>I had episodes of depersonalisation, mostly when it got dark in the evening, where I'd feel like I was dissolving back into that black space and that my life was the dream. During these episodes I'd have to grab something solid and say my name out loud.<br><br>Panic attacks came in small rooms and corridors with corners, like hotel corridors, basements, elevators. I'd feel like the walls were endless and I'd never find the way out.<br><br>I was depressed and also very angry, at myself, but mainly at the organiser who didn't come when I knocked and then made me wait another hour. I felt that he had treated my terror as a 'process' when I needed help.<br><br>My concentration was bad. I made mistakes at work. "Ein paar Wochen lang hatte ich Angst vor Herzrasen und habe staendig meinen Puls gemessen. Danach ging es wieder.",
```

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1290 columns across 106 data files.
#### Issues Identified

113 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 106 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

-  We assessed 15 R code files for reproducibility and ran 7 of them (each in an isolated Docker container).

live_data_statements: Simplified overview of the overall analysis pipeline employed in our study (acceptance-and avoidance-related) psychedelic experiences. Wolff et al. (2022) collected data from 2,078 participants; after applying the exclusion criteria of the original study, data from 1,829 participants remain (997 English-and 832 German-speaking), who each reported on one psychedelic experience (clearly discernible psychoactive effects) following the use of different substances (LSD, psilocybin, mescaline, or ayahuasca).
Participants were instructed that both positive and negative experiences could be reported on.
After questions on demographic data and mental health issues/diagnoses, participants were asked to describe the psychedelic experience in a free-text format, either in English or German.
A total of 1,195 volunteers began the survey and 512 provided informed consent to participate.

Of these, 269 participants were excluded for the following reasons: not meeting inclusion criteria (n = 90), discontinuation of the survey before completing the PCL-5 items (n = 176), free-text responses indicating a lack of genuine participation (e.g., "just reading"; n = 2), or exceeding the recommended relative speed index cut-off (> 2) without any indication of engagement in free-text comments (n = 1).
Participants were asked to report on this "particularly challenging or traumatic psychedelic experience", and additionally provided responses on a series of questions and questionnaires.

In a modification of the original instructions, participants were asked to rate their symptoms not over the past month, but specifically with reference to the month they found most challenging following their psychedelic experience.
Participants were asked three questions to which they were instructed to provide free-text responses: 1) Acute Symptoms.

Open-ended free-text responses function fundamentally different as they are inherently personalized: Depending on how open the questions are worded, participants are completely free to produce whatever they themselves deem relevant or informative.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 15 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:15, File = c("check_corpus.R", "config_data.R", 
"config.R", "datasets.R", "embed.R", "check_privacy.R", "export_tex.R", 
"extract_spec.R", "figures.R", "generate.R", "models.R", "nested.R", 
"overlap.R", "public_spec.R", "run_all.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "config_data.R", "—", "—", "config.R, embed.R, datasets.R", 
"—", "config.R, embed.R, datasets.R", "config_data.R", "config.R", 
"—", "—", "—", "—", "generate.R"), Basis = c("none", 
"none", "dependency", "none", "none", "dependency", "none", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "none", "none", "none", "none", "dependency"
)), row.names = c(NA, -15L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. The code reads files that are only inside `fguenther/free-text-analysis-psychedelics-v1.zip`, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as `unzip("free-text-analysis-psychedelics-v1.zip")` in R), or upload the files unpacked. **7 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files not run on their own
5 files only define functions, so running them on their own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("datasets.R", "embed.R", "models.R", 
"nested.R", "overlap.R"), "Used by" = c("embed.R, export_tex.R, models.R, overlap.R, check_privacy.R, extract_spec.R", 
"datasets.R, run_all.R, check_privacy.R, extract_spec.R", "export_tex.R, figures.R, nested.R, overlap.R, run_all.R", 
"run_all.R", "export_tex.R, run_all.R")), row.names = c(NA, -5L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 12 scripts: 3 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 5 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script needs a person** to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: check_privacy.R. Naming the file in the script solves this. **1 script needs the internet**, which is off during the run: run_all.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `figures.R` after `config_data.R`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Run by another script**

5 scripts are run by another script with `source()`, so they were not run on their own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on their own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Their outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

> round_pd <- function(R, tol = 1e-4) {
>   min_eig <- function(A) min(eigen(A, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values)
>   R0 <- round(R, 2)
>   out <- R0; method <- "rounded (already positive definite)"
>   if (min_eig(R0) <= tol) {
>     R1 <- as.matrix(nearPD(R0, corr = TRUE, keepDiag = TRUE, eig.tol = 1e-6, posd.tol = 1e-3)$mat)
>     shrink <- 1
>     repeat {
>       out <- round(R1 * shrink, 2); diag(out) <- 1
>       if (min_eig(out) > tol || shrink < 0.5) break
>       shrink <- shrink - 0.01
>     }
>     method <- sprintf("Matrix::nearPD after rounding, rounded again%s",
>                       if (shrink < 1) sprintf(", off-diagonals shrunk by %.0f%%", 100 * (1 - shrink)) else "")
>   }
>   dimnames(out) <- dimnames(R)
>   list(matrix = out, method = method, min_eigenvalue = round(min_eig(out), 4),
>        max_abs_change = round(max(abs(out - R0)), 2))
> }

>     empty        = "^$",
>     integer      = "^-?[0-9]+$",
>     dec_comma    = "^-?[0-9]+,[0-9]+$",

>   if (is.null(dim(hit))) hit <- matrix(hit, nrow = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, names(pats)))
>   cnt <- c(NA_value = sum(is.na(x)), colSums(hit), other = sum(!is.na(x) & rowSums(hit) == 0))
>   cnt <- cnt[cnt > 0]
>   dec <- x[!is.na(x) & grepl("^-?[0-9]*[,.][0-9]+$", x, useBytes = TRUE)]

text.text: Clinical studies regularly ask participants to describe their experiences in their own words.
These open-ended questions are included so that participants can report what they themselves consider relevant, and ideally researchers want to harvest this information.

In practice however, these responses are rarely analyzed and often effectively discarded, since translating them into a useful quantitative format for further analysis traditionally required trained coders or advanced technical skills.

Current transformer-based language models offer an appealing alternative option to quantify text: they internally represent any text input as high-dimensional numerical representations called text embeddings.
From available open-weight models, these text embeddings can be freely extracted on a local machine.
As text embeddings are just vectors of numbers, they can be plugged as predictors into standard statistical analyses.
Here, we applied this to three large datasets in which participants described their experiences in the context of psychedelic substance use.

We investigated whether text embeddings of these free-text descriptions improve cross-validated, held-out predictions of clinically relevant outcomes (well-being, change in well-being, change in psychological flexibility, post-traumatic symptom severity, post-traumatic growth) after we control for a range of other predictors capturing demographic information, the setting of the experience, and a series of questionnaire data.
We found reliable increases in predictive accuracy for three of the five outcomes (change in well-being and psychological flexibility, post-traumatic symptom severity), in two of the three datasets.
Some of these increases are substantial.

We therefore recommend (where possible) the inclusion of open-ended questions in any questionnaire, and to actually pass this information to analysis, to efficiently capture valuable information that would otherwise be lost.
In psychology, as in any empirical science, we rely on empirical data to test our hypotheses and draw theoretical conclusions.
These data come in different formats.

Much of the data used in our studies is inherently quantitative, collected as or straightforwardly converted into numbers, such as Likert-scale ratings in questionnaires, response times, or EEG signals; but also categorical data can be encoded via indicator variables with different coding schemes.

The disciplines of psychological methods, psychometrics, and diagnostics have developed sophisticated toolkits to deal with quantitative data, and much of our standard statistical toolkit as psychologists is tailored towards this data format.
In line with this, questionnaires often make heavy use of closed-form item formats, as exemplified by the aforementioned Likert-scales.
However, not all data is easily converted into quantitative data.
A prominent exception in psychology are free-text responses where participants answer a question verbally.

These are often presented as open-ended questions, without pre-defined response categories. 1 Language is the natural way for most humans to express their thoughts and feelings, and each of us has spent a lifetime mastering this specific medium of providing information to others (Kjell et al., 2023; Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010).
text.formatted: These are often presented as open-ended questions, without pre-defined response categories. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> Language is the natural way for most humans to express their thoughts and feelings, and each of us has spent a lifetime mastering this specific medium of providing information to others <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Kjell et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: From a data analysis side however, this data has long been notoriously difficult to deal with, which often resulted in gaps between study designs and data analyses: On the one hand, psychologists value free-text responses to open-ended questions (such as "Please describe your traumatic experience"), consider them informative, and consequently regularly include them in their questionnaires (Schuman & Presser, 1979; Singer & Couper, 2017).
text.formatted: From a data analysis side however, this data has long been notoriously difficult to deal with, which often resulted in gaps between study designs and data analyses: On the one hand, psychologists value free-text responses to open-ended questions (such as "Please describe your traumatic experience"), consider them informative, and consequently regularly include them in their questionnaires <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Schuman & Presser, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Singer & Couper, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This illustrates a clear belief on side of the researchers that there is valuable information in these free-text responses.
In open-ended free-text responses, participants can provide rich and varied reports about their unique experiences, problems, issues, and strategies.
Crucially, they can provide information they themselves deem important, and that the researcher may have missed to look out for with their data collection tools.
On the other hand however, this data usually does not enter the data analysis and is, effectively speaking, discarded (Roberts et al., 2014; Singer & Couper, 2017).
text.formatted: On the other hand however, this data usually does not enter the data analysis and is, effectively speaking, discarded <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Roberts et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Singer & Couper, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the valuable information assumed to be provided in these responses is simply lost.
Of course, data analysis techniques that turn free-text responses into quantitative data have been at our disposal for a long time.
A straightforward option is to encode them as categorical data.

This works as long as the set of response options is finite and thus not truly open-ended (e.g., "country of residence"), or if the vast majority of responses fall on a relatively restricted set and one is willing to accept an "other" category.

For more nuanced responses to truly open-ended questions such as "please describe your relationship to your mother", simply coding the responses as "good", "bad", "okay" is doing the participants and researchers a disservice.

To counteract this, more sophisticated annotation methods such as qualitative content analysis (Mayring, 2014) or thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006), often implemented in dedicated software such as MAXQDA (VERBI Software, 2024), have been developed.
text.formatted: To counteract this, more sophisticated annotation methods such as qualitative content analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mayring, 2014)</ref> or thematic analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Braun & Clarke, 2006)</ref>, often implemented in dedicated software such as MAXQDA (VERBI Software, 2024), have been developed.

text.text: While these are often regarded as qualitative rather than quantitative analysis techniques, this describes the annotation process more than the outcome: While it is indeed true that (trained human) annotators rely on qualitative judgments to develop the annotation schemes, a proper annotation can arrive at a quantitative (vector) representation of the text (with, for example, dimensions such as "single parent: 0/1").
The present study does not intend to pass judgment on the outcomes and quality of such techniques.
However, qualitative data analysis is a skill that requires intensive training, and that requires a lot of time to properly apply (Braun & Clarke, 2006; O'Connor & Joffe, 2020).
text.formatted: However, qualitative data analysis is a skill that requires intensive training, and that requires a lot of time to properly apply <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Braun & Clarke, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">O'Connor & Joffe, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: As coding categories may repeatedly have to be re-visited with new free-text data points, scalability to large datasets can also become a serious issue.
Automated alternatives exist, but come with their own limits.

Dictionary approaches such as LIWC (Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count; Boyd and Schwartz, 2021; Tausczik and Pennebaker, 2010) count words from pre-defined categories; these methods re-introduce a top-down filter that open-ended questions seek to avoid in the first place (Schwartz et al., 2013), are susceptible to surface-level word form variations in addition to the relevant semantic information, and largely ignore context information.
text.formatted: Dictionary approaches such as LIWC <ref type="bibr">(Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Boyd and Schwartz, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Tausczik and Pennebaker, 2010)</ref> count words from pre-defined categories; these methods re-introduce a top-down filter that open-ended questions seek to avoid in the first place <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Schwartz et al., 2013)</ref>, are susceptible to surface-level word form variations in addition to the relevant semantic information, and largely ignore context information.

text.text: Topic models (Blei et al., 2003; Roberts et al., 2014) need large corpora and mainly describe what is discussed, not whether it adds predictive information.
text.formatted: Topic models <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blei et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Roberts et al., 2014)</ref> need large corpora and mainly describe what is discussed, not whether it adds predictive information.

text.text: Supervised classifiers, finally, require manually annotated training data.
The often small sample sizes typical of clinical studies can place strong limitations on the applicability of such methods.
Current developments in Natural Language Processing (NLP), the AI/machine learning discipline concerned with quantifying text data, offer a promising solution to these issues.

Over the last years, the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) could not be overlooked (Brown et al., 2020; Demszky et al., 2023), and it is increasingly clear that these models develop good representations of the text presented to them.
text.formatted: Over the last years, the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) could not be overlooked <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Brown et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Demszky et al., 2023)</ref>, and it is increasingly clear that these models develop good representations of the text presented to them.

text.text: Critically for our purposes, we can access these internal representations.

The engine of modern LLMs remains the transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017), a very deep neural network that at its core is trained to predict missing or upcoming tokens (which can be words but also sub-word units) based on the tokens already present in the input (for example, prompts that users provide to the model; Brown et al., 2020; Devlin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The engine of modern LLMs remains the transformer architecture <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Vaswani et al., 2017)</ref>, a very deep neural network that at its core is trained to predict missing or upcoming tokens (which can be words but also sub-word units) based on the tokens already present in the input (for example, prompts that users provide to the model; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Brown et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Devlin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: As a neural network, the transformer represents its input as numbers (a binary vector which words are present in the input), which are repeatedly transformed into other vectors through a series of complex operations (for overviews, see for example Cassani et al., 2024; Günther and Cassani, 2026) before eventually arriving at a probability distribution for the prediction of the missing/upcoming token.
text.formatted: As a neural network, the transformer represents its input as numbers (a binary vector which words are present in the input), which are repeatedly transformed into other vectors through a series of complex operations (for overviews, see for example <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cassani et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Günther and Cassani, 2026)</ref> before eventually arriving at a probability distribution for the prediction of the missing/upcoming token.

text.text: Critically, these "other vectors" -the so-called text embeddings -are the model's internal representations of the input text that enable it to successfully perform its task.

For our purposes, this provides us with quantitative representations of any input text as text embeddings (that is, vectors of numbers) which we can then plug into our familiar quantitative data analysis techniques (Debelak et al., 2025; Kjell et al., 2019 Kjell et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: For our purposes, this provides us with quantitative representations of any input text as text embeddings (that is, vectors of numbers) which we can then plug into our familiar quantitative data analysis techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Debelak et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kjell et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kjell et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: Since such embeddings are extracted from large and general pre-trained models without any fine-tuning on or adjustment to the data of a given study, they are available even for single pieces of text, and thus also for free-text responses in studies with small sample sizes.

In the present study, we demonstrate that this allows us to establish automated pipelines to utilize free-text responses in clinical studies, without requiring any human annotation (see also Eichstaedt et al., 2018; Kjell et al., 2022).

text.text: We show that making use of the rich information contained in free-text responses allows us to achieve sometimes substantial gains in predictive accuracy even when we consider large sets of other predictors, for relevant clinical outcomes, such as psychological well-being or post-traumatic symptom severity.

In the analysis of the APEQ data, our main outcome variable of interest is the change in subjective well-being (assessed via the WHO-5 well-being index, Topp et al., 2015) from before to after the psychedelic experience.

text.text: Both the "before" and "after" rating were assessed retrospectively by the participants, and the change score was computed as the difference between the two scores.

Subjective well-being is an ideal outcome variable in this setting: On the one hand, it is a very general variable that is influenced by many different factors (Dolan et al., 2008); on the other hand, as a measure of general life satisfaction, it is of immediate practical importance to practitioners and patients.

Free-text responses.
After questions on demographic data and mental health issues/diagnoses, participants were asked to describe the psychedelic experience in a free-text format, either in English or German.
This free-text data is available from 958 participants (526 English-speaking, 432 German-speaking).
Only data from these 958 participants is passed on to further analysis.

Free-text responses.
In free-text responses, participants described the impact of the psychedelic experience on (a) their handling of stressful events, and (b) on their mental health.
We thus have two different free-text responses available here, describing related but potentially different topics.
Such free-text data is available from 605 participants (401 English-speaking, 204 German-speaking; roughly 2/3 of the dataset used for the APEQ analysis).
Only data from these 605 participants is passed on to further analysis.
