text.text: After minimal text cleaning in the raw data (removal of names and personal contact data; removal of three random character strings), we extracted sentence embeddings (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019) for the free-text responses using the R package reticulate (Ushey et al., 2026).
text.formatted: After minimal text cleaning in the raw data (removal of names and personal contact data; removal of three random character strings), we extracted sentence embeddings <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Reimers & Gurevych, 2019)</ref> for the free-text responses using the R package reticulate <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Ushey et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, as free-text responses are available in different languages (German and English), we selected the intfloat/multilingual-e5-large model (Wang et al., 2024) from the Hugging Face platform (https://huggingface.co/intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), which produces 1,024-dimensional embeddings for each text in 24 model layers.
text.formatted: In particular, as free-text responses are available in different languages (German and English), we selected the intfloat/multilingual-e5-large model <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Wang et al., 2024)</ref> from the Hugging Face platform (<ref type="url" target="https://huggingface.co/intfloat/multilingual-e5-large">https://huggingface.co/intfloat/multilingual-e5-large</ref>), which produces 1,024-dimensional embeddings for each text in 24 model layers.

text.text: A robustness check with the BAAI/bge-m3 model (J. Chen et al., 2024) that arrives at very similar results as the main analysis is presented in the Supplementary Material.
text.formatted: A robustness check with the BAAI/bge-m3 model (J. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Chen et al., 2024</ref>) that arrives at very similar results as the main analysis is presented in the Supplementary Material.

text.text: As open model weights are downloaded from Hugging Face to a local machine for extracting text embeddings, the model runs fully offline, no third-party API is involved, and participant responses are not sent to any third party as part of this process.
In datasets where we have multiple free-text responses (2 in the GCMQ data: events and health; 3 in the PTSD data: acute, post-acute, and treat), we embedded each of them separately.
With the model's context length of 512 tokens, almost all the free-text responses could be fully embedded; longer responses were truncated 2 .

In line with the multilingual-e5-large model setup, the prefix "passage:" was prepended to all responses before extracting the embeddings(for comparability, this was also done for the bge-m3 model, so that the two analyses differ only in the embedding model).

Following the conventional approach (e.g., Kjell et al., 2023), we used the embeddings in the final hidden layer of the model (before the output layer), where the embeddings are fully contextualized and make use of all learned weights of the model, for further analysis.
text.formatted: Following the conventional approach (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kjell et al., 2023)</ref>, we used the embeddings in the final hidden layer of the model (before the output layer), where the embeddings are fully contextualized and make use of all learned weights of the model, for further analysis.

text.text: As implemented in the sentence-transformers library, a single embedding per response was obtained by averaging over the token embeddings (multilingual-e5-large) or by taking the embedding of the initial [CLS] token (bge-m3), and normalized to unit length.
Sentence transformers produce high-dimensional representations to be able to adequately represent the vast variety of possible text (and their semantic content) that can occur in natural language.

However, free-text responses describing psychedelic experiences will usually not cover the whole range of possible semantic content, and so 1,024 distinct numerical predictors for each text will not be required in our setup.
In addition, text embedding dimensions can be highly collinear, especially for thematically related texts.
We therefore ran a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) over all text embeddings from an individual set of free-text responses, and only retained the 20 first principal components.
This number was held constant across all analyses for consistency.
A parameter sweep for different numbers of principal components is presented in the Supplementary Material.
Note that the PCA ran within the folds of the cross-validation (next section).

The central question of the present study is whether we can gain additional predictive accuracy in statistical analyses by considering the information provided in participants' free-text responses, in the form of automatically-extracted text embeddings without any additional (human) annotation.

Thus, our main focus lies on prediction, rather than interpretations of individual model parameter estimates (Shmueli, 2010; Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017) -especially since the dimensions of text embeddings are usually not directly interpretable but require additional analyses (e.g., Kjell et al., 2019 Kjell et al., , 2023)).
text.formatted: Thus, our main focus lies on prediction, rather than interpretations of individual model parameter estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Shmueli, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Yarkoni & Westfall, 2017)</ref> -especially since the dimensions of text embeddings are usually not directly interpretable but require additional analyses (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kjell et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Kjell et al., , 2023))</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, our metric of interest is incremental validity -that is, increases in variance explained ∆R² when predictor variables from text embeddings are included as additional predictors in cross-validated regression models that are designed to counteract over-fitting.

For a schematic overview of the analysis pipeline, see again Depending on the number k of free-text responses in a dataset, we will have a nested hierarchy of such extended-by-text models, as will be described in detail in the individual sections below.
All regression models were estimated using elastic net regression (Zou & Hastie, 2005).
text.formatted: All regression models were estimated using elastic net regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Zou & Hastie, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Elastic net is a regularization technique that combines ridge and lasso penalties to shrink (ridge) and, where appropriate, eliminate (lasso) coefficients.
This renders it useful to counter-act overfitting in datasets with many, potentially correlated predictors.

Model performance for each elastic net model was evaluated using repeated nested cross-validation using the R package caret (Kuhn, 2008): In the outer loop, the data were split into 10 folds; for each fold, the model was trained and model coefficients estimated on 90% of the data, and the resulting model was then used to generate predictions for the remaining 10% held-out data which the model has not seen during training.
text.formatted: Model performance for each elastic net model was evaluated using repeated nested cross-validation using the R package caret <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Kuhn, 2008)</ref>: In the outer loop, the data were split into 10 folds; for each fold, the model was trained and model coefficients estimated on 90% of the data, and the resulting model was then used to generate predictions for the remaining 10% held-out data which the model has not seen during training.

text.text: The PCA on the text embedding dimensions ran on the training data only, and the coefficients from the training set were then used to project the embeddings of the test set into the same lower-dimensional space (i.e., perform dimensionality reduction).
This process repeated across all folds, and the whole procedure was repeated 10 times with different random assignments of participants to folds (i.e., 10 × 10 outer folds in total).
The squared correlation between predicted and observed values in each held-out fold, averaged over all outer folds, constitutes the cross-validated (held-out) R² (Kuhn, 2008).
text.formatted: The squared correlation between predicted and observed values in each held-out fold, averaged over all outer folds, constitutes the cross-validated (held-out) R² <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Kuhn, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The elastic net hyperparameters (the mixing parameter α and penalty strength λ) were tuned via grid search (hyperparameter ranges: α ∈ [0, 1], 11 values in steps of 0.1; λ ∈ [10 -4 , 10 1 ], 100 log-spaced values), in an inner loop: Within each outer training set, we ran a 5-fold cross-validation (again with the PCA computed on the inner training data only), selected the combination of α and λ yielding the highest inner cross-validated R² , and then re-fitted the model with these values on the whole outer training set.

The held-out data of an outer fold were thus used neither for estimating the coefficients nor for selecting the hyperparameters, so that the cross-validated R² is not inflated by the hyperparameter selection (Varma & Simon, 2006).
text.formatted: The held-out data of an outer fold were thus used neither for estimating the coefficients nor for selecting the hyperparameters, so that the cross-validated R² is not inflated by the hyperparameter selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Varma & Simon, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Note that different values of α and λ can thus be applied for the baseline model and the extended-by-text models (as well as in different outer folds; we report their median across the outer folds).

As our aim is to assess how much predictive information can be gauged from the predictor variables, and not how the regression models perform under exactly the same hyperparameter settings, this choice aligns with our study objectives.

As noted above, the difference in cross-validated R² between the model with and without text-embedding predictors (∆R² , also referred to as incremental validity; Hunsley and Meyer, 2003; Sechrest, 1963 ) serves as the index of the added predictive value of the free-text data.

text.text: To test whether the free-text data reliably increase predictive accuracy, we compared each extended-by-text model with the baseline model on the same outer folds (all models for one outcome variable were evaluated on identical outer and inner folds).
For each outer fold j, we computed the difference d j between the held-out R² of the two models; ∆R² is the mean of these J = 10 × 10 differences.
Since the training sets of different folds overlap, the d j are not independent, and a standard paired t-test would underestimate their variance.
We therefore used a corrected repeated k-fold t-test (Bouckaert & Frank, 2004; Nadeau & Bengio, 2003), and report 95% confidence intervals based on the same corrected standard error.
text.formatted: We therefore used a corrected repeated k-fold t-test <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bouckaert & Frank, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Nadeau & Bengio, 2003)</ref>, and report 95% confidence intervals based on the same corrected standard error.

text.text: In datasets with more than one free-text response, we pre-specified the extended-by-text model containing all free-text responses as the test of incremental validity; the models with other combinations of responses are reported descriptively (their p-values are not corrected for multiple comparisons).

That being said, for differences in well-being (WHO-5), the examples in Table 3 suggest quite clearly that the best-improving positive shifts are found where the free-text responses describe positive emotions following the substance use: relaxation, intense positive feelings of happiness, symptoms relief in affective disorders, and general life satisfaction.

On the other hand, the best-improving negative shifts (that is, decreases in the outcome variable) are found when the free-text responses describe insights and (meta-)cognitive processes, especially evaluations and judgments: increased awareness for oneself and ones own mental states, as well as the (social) environment.
So interestingly, the free-text responses associated with positive and negative shifts are not polar opposites on one semantic dimension.

In a qualitative interpretation, it is striking that strong negative prediction shifts are often associated to responses that describe indifference -here, it seems that the regression model based on the other predictors otherwise overshoots in its predictions of well-being.

Beyond that, other responses associated to strong negative shifts describe (too) short-lived effects, or no impact of the experience (here, the model predictions based on the other predictors appear to otherwise overshoot).
Strong positive shifts on the other hand are often associated to responses describing euphoria, connectedness and love, open-mindedness, and newly-found appreciation of life.

In a qualitative interpretation, free-text responses with very positive shift values (i.e., increases in symptom severity) for the most part simply describe (severe) symptoms of mental disorders across the board, and not restricted to PTSD symptoms.
It may not be too surprising that this information helps predicting PTSD symptom severity.
Free-text responses with very negative shift values (i.e., decreases in symptom severity) mostly state that there were no persistent difficulties, or describe insights about oneself.
Free-text responses are frequently collected in clinical studies, but are often not analyzed systematically and rigorously.

In the present study, we investigated to what extent the information in participant's free-text responses can be harvested with text embedding models to increase the held-out predictive accuracy for relevant outcome measures above and beyond sizable collections of standard predictors (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: In the present study, we investigated to what extent the information in participant's free-text responses can be harvested with text embedding models to increase the held-out predictive accuracy for relevant outcome measures above and beyond sizable collections of standard predictors (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: Specifically, we investigated free-text responses describing experiences associated with psychedelic substance use, in addition to demographic predictors, setting variables, and series of questionnaire scores.

Across three large datasets (Evens et al., 2026; Wolff et al., 2022 Wolff et al., , 2024) ) with five different outcome measures, the increase in predictive accuracy is sometimes substantial (Table 1): We find significant increases in predictive accuracy between around 3% and 10% for predicting changes in subjective well-being (APEQ WHO-5), changes in psychological flexibility (APEQ AAQ-II) and post-traumatic stress disorder symptom severity (PTSD PCL-5).

text.text: As the variances explained range around 30% to 40%, these increases matter.
However, such result patterns are not ubiquitous: For well-being (GCMQ WEMWBS) and post-traumatic growth (PTSD PTGI), we find no significant increases.
These results replicate in a robustness check with a second text embedding model (bge-m3 ; see the Supplementary Material).
As can be seen in Table 2, overlap between text embeddings and other predictors is generally small to moderate.

text.text: The free-text responses thus contain information not captured by the other measurement tools.

Qualitative inspections suggest that the most predictive free-text responses contain a broad range of relatively straightforward information: emotional reactions, indifference, meta-cognitive processes, or symptoms of mental disorders.

Notably, in our reading the predictive texts mainly convey psychological information on the participant's own cognitive and emotional states, rather than information about the outside world (such as events or settings).

Concerning the GCMQ results, it may be initially tempting to attribute the lower ∆R² to the much larger number of other predictors considered in the analysis (which stems from the fact that more such predictors are available in the dataset).
However, in Table 1 one can clearly see that the ∆R² values in the model comparisons are very much aligned with the R² values of the text-only models.
text.formatted: However, in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> one can clearly see that the ∆R² values in the model comparisons are very much aligned with the R² values of the text-only models.

text.text: Sample size is also not the determinant of these findings -the sample size of the PTSD-PCL-5 data is below half of the GCMQ data, but the ∆R² is much higher.
And within the PTSD data, ∆R² differs substantially between the two different outcomes PCL-5 and PTGI, even though the set of baseline predictors is identical.
This indicates that in cases like the GCMQ data (or the PTSD-PTGI data), the text genuinely carries less information about the outcomes.

One potential reason for the discrepancy between the APEQ-WHO-5 and the GCMQ(-WEMWBS) results, where both outcome variables are well-being measures, may be the different nature of the free-text responses: In the GCMQ data, participants do not describe the experience itself, but its perceived impact on stress handling and mental health.

However, there are also other differences: WEMWBS in the GCMQ data is a state-level variable of current well-being, while WHO-5 in the APEQ data is a retrospective assessment of the difference in well-being before and after the psychedelic experience.

Also R² is generally lower for all models in the GCMQ data than in the APEQ data (which may be a consequence of the different types of outcome variables, as most baseline predictors of the APEQ models are also included in the GCMQ models, with the exception of duration, mood, preparedness, strength of the effects, and the APEQ-ACE ×

In the PTSD-PTGI data, the most reasonable conclusion to us is that the free-text responses just do not carry information about posttraumatic growth, in particular because the questions focused on symptoms.

As the question did not ask for posttraumatic growth, and many participants may not have experienced this or may not even be aware of the concept, findings such as these are bound to occur -as any other variable, free-text responses will not be a universal predictor of every possible outcome.

In addition, the concept and its measurement itself have received criticism in the literature Frazier et al., 2009; Jayawickreme et al., 2021, which may lead to difficulties in predicting this variable.

text.text: The role of open-ended free-text responses

Of course, analyses of free-text responses are and have been performed already (Mayring, 2014), often requiring highly effortful and resource-intensive human annotation Braun and Clarke, 2006; O'Connor and Joffe, 2020.
text.formatted: Of course, analyses of free-text responses are and have been performed already <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mayring, 2014)</ref>, often requiring highly effortful and resource-intensive human annotation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Braun and Clarke, 2006</ref>; O'Connor and Joffe, 2020.

text.text: As a direct consequence, there are serious issues with scalability to large datasetsfoot_2 .
text.formatted: As a direct consequence, there are serious issues with scalability to large datasets<ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">foot_2</ref> .

text.text: In contrast, applying techniques from machine learning/NLP is often just a matter of seconds or maybe minutes.

Such techniques have been available for some time, for example using word counts (Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010), but also vector representation models such as Latent Semantic Analysis or word2vec have already been used to analyze free-text responses also in clinical settings Barattieri di San Pietro et al., 2023; De Boer et al., 2018; Elvevåg et al., 2007; Kintsch, 2002. With context-aware text embeddings models, where texts are no longer treated as an unordered bag of words, this vector space approach has become far more sophisticated and powerful.
text.formatted: Such techniques have been available for some time, for example using word counts <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Tausczik & Pennebaker, 2010)</ref>, but also vector representation models such as Latent Semantic Analysis or word2vec have already been used to analyze free-text responses also in clinical settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Barattieri di San Pietro et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">De Boer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Elvevåg et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kintsch, 2002.</ref> With context-aware text embeddings models, where texts are no longer treated as an unordered bag of words, this vector space approach has become far more sophisticated and powerful.

text.text: Text embeddings do not annotate a set of defined criteria, but instead are general-level quantitative representations of the text and its meaning.

This has the disadvantage that these embeddings are not directly interpretable, but the advantage that they encode whatever the participant produced without requiring a top-down filter of search criteria.
Concerning the disadvantage of initial non-interpretability, this is one that can be addressed.

Common approaches cluster analyses on text embeddings that allow researchers to assess common themes and topics (Grootendorst, 2022; Lalk et al., 2024), or regression-based approaches to predict pre-defined semantic dimensions such as valence from text embeddings (Gatti et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Common approaches cluster analyses on text embeddings that allow researchers to assess common themes and topics <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Grootendorst, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lalk et al., 2024)</ref>, or regression-based approaches to predict pre-defined semantic dimensions such as valence from text embeddings <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gatti et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, our approach to establish interpretability was to examine the responses that contributed the most to making the predictions more accurate (i.e., decreased residuals the most).
As showcased in the Results sections, this reveals valuable information provided by participants, and common themes in their responses.

This ties in to a more general point about free-text responses: In standard questionnaire items the researcher has to determine which construct they aim to measure (and ideally then evaluate the item), and the item then serves as a "fishing net" to catch exactly that construct.

Open-ended free-text responses function fundamentally different as they are inherently personalized: Depending on how open the questions are worded, participants are completely free to produce whatever they themselves deem relevant or informative.
The selection is thus passed from researcher to participant.

In the words of Schwartz et al. (2013), "the data itself drives a comprehensive exploration of language that distinguishes people, finding connections that are not captured with traditional closed-vocabulary word-category analyses" (see also Boyd and Schwartz, 2021).
text.formatted: In the words of <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Schwartz et al. (2013)</ref>, "the data itself drives a comprehensive exploration of language that distinguishes people, finding connections that are not captured with traditional closed-vocabulary word-category analyses" (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Boyd and Schwartz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This opens up a very simple opportunity to catch information we might otherwise have missed, because (to stay in the metaphor), the meshes of the fishing net were too large, or the net was in a wrong place entirely.
We do not want to claim that no questionnaire items can be developed to catch this information -this possibility surely exists (the net can be changed or moved).

In our qualitative examinations of what responses increase predictive accuracy, the relevant dimensions appear to be rather obvious, for example describing evaluations, meta-cognitive processes, or symptoms of mental disorders.

Still, even though seemingly similar items existed in the questionnaires (for example, about the valence and retrospective appraisal of the psychedelic experience), these apparently did not capture the relevant information.
This demonstrates that open-ended free-text responses can always function as a convenient back-up to capture information that could otherwise be missed.
This is especially relevant in data collection scenarios where one cannot or does not want to let the participants fill in questionnaires for hours.

As argued by (Kjell et al., 2019 (Kjell et al., , 2022)), participants also often perceive the free-text response format as more natural than standard questionnaire items which force them to translate some subjective experience into a single number.
text.formatted: As argued by <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kjell et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kjell et al., , 2022))</ref>, participants also often perceive the free-text response format as more natural than standard questionnaire items which force them to translate some subjective experience into a single number.

text.text: Open-ended questions with free-text responses may also address issues with suggestive questions in research surveys.

In research on psychedelic experiences, there is currently a debate that standard questionnaire items can push participants to focus on specific dimensions of their experience and reinforce stereotypical perspectives, which can bias the data (Vanderijst et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In research on psychedelic experiences, there is currently a debate that standard questionnaire items can push participants to focus on specific dimensions of their experience and reinforce stereotypical perspectives, which can bias the data <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Vanderijst et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Open-ended questions can be formulated very generically ("Describe your psychedelic experience"), so that such biases can be largely avoided.
Based on our study, our practical recommendation is to include at least one open-ended question with a free-text response format into any questionnaire.
Even if it just "Is there anything else you want to tell us?"
with an obligatory response field that requires a minimal amount of characters, there may always be useful information that would otherwise be missed.

Text embeddings -from open, locally-run models to ensure data protection -make it very convenient to analyze such responses, so researchers do not have to worry about time-and resource-intensive annotation steps.
The analysis pipeline presented in the present article can serve as a template for this (see also Debelak et al., 2025; Kjell et al., 2023).

text.text: Similar methods can, and have been, applied for clinical diagnoses -for example, researchers have used patients' free-text data from interviews of spontaneous speech as the input for classifiers trained to perform clinical diagnoses (Agbavor & Liang, 2022; F. Chen et al., 2025 F. Chen et al., , 2026)).

Chen et al., 2025</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">F. Chen et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Of course, if more specific questions are included -such as the questions to describe the psychedelic experiences in our current study -this can only add more information.
Depending on the research question and the data collection setting, this introduces a tradeoff question between time and resources invested and informative data points collected.

As the human communicative system has developed under evolutionary pressure to efficiently convey rich information (Gibson et al., 2019), we suspect that this tradeoff may often play out in favor of open-ended free-text responses.

AI tools (Claude Code; Sonnet and Opus, versions 5 and 5.5) were used on toy data to streamline and better structure the scripts, to adapt the script for all datasets and outcome variables, to create a structured and reproducible repository that flows into a reproducible L A T E Xdocument, and for literature search.

No AI tools were used for writing the first complete version of the manuscript text; AI tools were then used to implement selected changes to the methods and analysis after internal revisions, and draft the corresponding suggestions for changes to Methods and Results.
All AI-suggested modifications were manually reviewed and validated by the first author.

text.text: These results are based on a single (non-repeated, non-nested) 10-fold cross-validation run, as repeating the nested cross-validation for every number of components would have been computationally prohibitive.

As the hyperparameters are selected on the same folds that are used for evaluation here, these R² values tend to be optimistic compared to the nested results in the main text (hardly in the APEQ data, but more clearly in the GCMQ data and especially in the comparatively small PTSD dataset); the informative part is therefore the comparison across numbers of components.

In the APEQ and GCMQ data, R² increases steeply up to about 10-15 components and remains largely stable up to about 40 components before slowly decreasing; the 20 components used in the main analysis lie within this stable range.
For PCL-5 in the PTSD data, the pattern is similar but noisier.
For PTGI, no number of components leads to an increase over the baseline model.

Figure 3 presents the same information for the bge-m3 embeddings, where we find comparable results, with one exception: for PCL-5, R² continues to increase up to 40-60 components, so that the main analysis with 20 components is, if anything, conservative here (although the gains at larger numbers of components, estimated on fewer than 210 training participants, are particularly prone to the optimism described above).

text.text: PTGI scores are only available from 230 participants, of which 229 are analysed (for one participant, one of the other predictors is missing).

To assess the added predictive accuracy brought about by free-text data, we estimated nested regression models for each outcome variable: The main analysis relies on a baseline model containing what has been defined in the Method sections as "other predictor variables" (the upper, blue track of Figure1), and "extended-by-text" models that additionally include the 20 text-embedding principal components for a specific free-text response (the rightmost, purple part of Figure1, combining the blue and orange tracks).

it is also evident that information encoded in the text data (a) goes far beyond what these questionnaires measure, and (b) this additional information is useful for predicting differences in the outcome variables.
differences in psychological flexibility (AAQ-II), the most-improving responses are presented in Table 4.
Note again that positive changes indicate a decrease in flexibility, while negative changes indicate an increase in flexibility.

The pattern here is thus in line with what we observe for the WHO-5 prediction: Reports of self-awareness, re-evaluation, and meta-cognition are associated to more positive changes (= decreases) in psychological flexibility, while reports of content, serenity, and happiness are associated to more negative changes (= increases).

The very points discussed so far also come with limitations: Since participants choose what responses they provide and what type of information they present in their responses, there is very little researcher control.
For instance, even a single participant response will likely often not focus on a single construct or concept, but touch on different, possibly only loosely related or unrelated concepts.
The same will likely apply for responses collected from different participants, who may choose to focus on entirely different aspects of a topic or even entirely different topics.
Depending on the research question and objective, this may introduce unacceptable noise to the study.
Additionally, open-ended response by their nature often prevent the researcher from cleanly pre-defining the construct or concept they are supposed to measure.
This makes them a risky or often unusable choice for confirmatory hypothesis-testing, where a specific relation between specific variables is at the center of the research question.
